subtopic: EMPLOYER-EMPLOYEE COUNCIL-PERSONNEL OF INITIAL COUNCIL OF SIXTEEN

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EMPLOYER-EMPLOYEE COUNCIL-PERSONNEL OF INITIAL COUNCIL OF SIXTEEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a statement regarding the national joint council of the public service of Canada. The house will recall that on February 24 I announced that the treasury board had decided to establish such a council in order to provide machinery for regular and systematic consultation and discussion between the employer and employee sides of the public service in regard to grievances and conditions of employment, and thereby to promote increased efficiency and better morale in the public service.
It has been found that it takes longer to get such organizations established than originally contemplated. However, it is only natural that in an organization as large and complicated as the government service there should be many differences of opinion as to the composition of such a council and the representation to be given to various groups or organizations in the civil service.
We originally intended to provide for a council of twelve, equally representative of the official or employer side and the staff or employee side of the public service, and therefore announced that the Civil Service Federation, the Civil Service Association, the Amalgamated Civil Servants, the Professional Institute and the Dominion Customs and Excise Officers' Association would each be asked to name one representative, and that the three organizations amongst the postal employees would be asked to name one to represent all postal employees. Following my announcement of February 24, we received representations from the three organizations in the postal service protesting that no single person chosen from one of them could fairly represent the three organizations, and insisting on each organization being allowed to name its own representative. While this would mean a council somewhat unwieldy in size, nevertheless the treasury board decided that as the main purpose was to promote good will and better understanding, it should accede to the request. The board was immediately criticized for this decision, primarily on the general ground that it would give too much weight to what were strictly departmental organizations within the Post Office Department. At the same time we received requests for representation from several other civil service organizations, some recently

Public Service Council-Personnel
formed, which, if they were all accepted, would lead to the establishment of a council of no less than twenty-four members.
The board has therefore come to the conclusion that these differences and difficulties as to representation can only be adjusted amicably as a result of full and frank discussion of the whole matter between representatives of the various organizations and the official side of the civil service. In this connection I would emphasize that the first main task of the council will be to consider carefully the tentative or preliminary constitution which is being laid down by the order in council and to recommend a permanent constitution to govern the activities of the council.
It will also have to consider the advisability of setting up departmental joint councils and it is believed that when members of the council have had a chance of threshing out the part which departmental councils should play and what their relation should be to the national joint council, it will be far easier to reach agreement as to the organizations which should be represented on the national council and the weight of their representation.
The treasury board is hopeful that in this way a plan can be worked out which will assure a workable constitution with fair and appropriate representation to all existing organizations, and to all elements of the public service in the national council and the departmental councils that may be recommended.
At the conclusion of my remarks I shall table the order in council which has been passed. It will provide initially for a council of sixteen members. The eight members from the staff or employee side who have been nominated by their respective organizations or associations are the following:

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: POSSIBILITY OF EXPEDITING THE INTRODUCTION OF PROPOSED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
I should like to ask the government if they will expedite as much as possible the bringing down of the remainder of the legislation which has been mentioned from time to time during the session and in the speech from the throne. I bring this to the attention of the government in order that we may be

Business oj the House-Legislation
able to make the best use of the time at our disposal in dealing with the activities of the session.
I find that apart altogether from the resolutions and second readings of certain bills that appear on the order paper, the following legislation is still to be brought down. When I read the list it will give hon. members some idea of what is ahead of us and how we must utilize our time if we are to make the most of it. The list is as follows: Civil service superannuation bill, amendment to Naval Services Act, Quebec Savings bank bill, export credit bill, national housing bill, the family allowances bill, floor prices for agriculture bill, war surplus assets bill, amendment to the Dominion Elections Act, Veterans' Gratuities bill, amendment to Veterans' Land Act, amendments to the criminal code, amendment to the Chinese Immigration Act, contributory old age pensions bill, health insurance bill; and in addition to these any legislation that may be based on reports of committees. Then there are the budget resolutions and whatever legislation may follow from them. In so far as the war appropriation bill is concerned the large departments of Agriculture, External Affairs, Finance, Pensions and National Health and Trade and Commerce have yet to be disposed of, plus thirteen separate items in other departments. If we continue to sit in future as we have done up to now, we have forty-three sitting days to August 1. We have had fifty-nine sitting days so far. I bring this to the attention of the house and of the government to request the government to expedite the bringing down of the legislation I have mentioned and thereby save time.
I should like to mention the cancellation of the Wednesday sittings. I do not want to bring up this matter ad nauseam, but I do feel keenly about it. I felt that the change should never have been made. But at this late date the government might give some consideration to the use of not only the Wednesday afternoons but Wednesday evenings, if they can possibly do it. This matter has been discussed and our party is substantially in agreement upon it. I may say to the government that as a party we are prepared to cooperate in these matters, and we hope that the government will do what it can-we shall do what we can-to bring the session into such order that the least possible time will be consumed in the transaction of the country's business. I realize it is not possible to cut off sessions at a certain time. This house owes a duty and an obligation to the country to see that legislation is dealt with properly. Subject to that reservation we as a party are anxious to see the session concluded as speedily as possible. I make this
suggestion in the hope that the tempo of the session may be increased and that the business of the country shall be carried on with perhaps even more dispatch than has been the case up to now.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Acting Prime Minister) :
subtopic: POSSIBILITY OF EXPEDITING THE INTRODUCTION OF PROPOSED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
I am obliged to my hon. friend for having brought up this matter. I have been sitting here during the last two or three weeks as the discussions have proceeded on the war appropriation resolution. I have once or twice made suggestions to the effect that I thought we might get on faster with better organization of the house. I felt that the remarks which I had made had fallen on barren ground and I thought I was putting the government in the position of endeavouring to force people to go faster than they wanted to go. I feel, however, that perhaps the course the government has pursued in just allowing the discussions to take their course has had some results. I take my hon. friend's words at their face value, that he is desirous of expediting the business of the house, as I am sure all hon. members are; but I think the example we have seen, in the length of time that has been taken on the war appropriation measure, is perhaps the best way to bring us to a realization that this house is a long way from having completed its business, and that some measures must be taken which, to use my hon. friend's expression, will speed up the tempo of the house.
I am not criticizing anyone, but it seems to me that is exactly what is needed here. As a matter of fact to-morrow, which is Wednesday, the day to which my hon. friend referred, I was going to ask the leader of the opposition and the leaders of the other two groups to a conference to see if it would not be possible to organize the discussion of these war appropriation items so that we might give some definite time to them and then call it a day when that time has expired. I know how difficult it is to do this. Hon. members want to ask questions which may occur to them at the moment when they happen to be in the house, and if they are away they want to be able to ask those questions after they come back, but that is not the way to get on with our business. So that I am going to ask my hon. friends to consider between now and to-morrow, if they will, the possibility of deciding on a certain number of hours, or a day if necessary., to deal with a certain subject and let us get it over and done with. It seems to me that is the only way we can speed up the tempo of the house.
With regard to the matter of legislation, it has seemed hardly worth while to place on the order paper a great deal of legislation which
Halibut Fisheries

may not be reached for one, two or three months in view of the speed we are making at the present time. The government has that matter fully in mind and legislation will be brought down from time to time; but with the situation as we have it, that is to say with the war appropriation measure still to be passed, a measure which I hope and believe we all regard as the most important of the session; with the farm improvement measure, which my hon. friend said he would like very much to have go to the banking and commerce committee in order that it might be considered along with the Bank Act; with some other legislation that has to come in and with the budget, which will be taken up in the reasonably near future, it seemed to me we had a pretty full order paper before us as it is. However, that legislation is in course of preparation; as a matter of fact most of it is prepared and can be brought down very shortly.
With regard to the matter of Wednesday, that has been discussed and I am not going to add anything to what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said in regard to it. I wish to close, however, by expressing appreciation of my hon. friend's having brought up the matter in a very graphic way, perhaps better than I could have done myself, because it comes from those who really have it in their own hands to decide how much time shall be taken on these matters. I thank him for having put on record again the programme we have ahead of us before this session would conclude in the normal course.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext: The house resumed from Monday, May 15, consideration in committee of a resolution to grant to His Majesty certain sums of money for the carrying out of measures consequent upon the existence of a state of war-Mr. Ilsley-Mr. Bradette in the chair.
Chief architect's branch-repairs, alterations, operation and maintenance of buildings occupied for war purposes, $2,300,000.
War Appropriation-Public Works

Before the first item is put to the committee, I am going to exercise a right which I believe I have. I hesitated to bring the matter up on a question of privilege because it has to do with a matter referred to in this debate, although it does not come under the Department of Public Works. On Friday, May 12-page 2865 of Hansard-the hon. member for New Westminster made the following statement with reference to the C.C.F.:
They went to the newspapers in the Fraser Valley and told them that in their party they had so many subscribers to these different papers, and they said, "If you do not give us an extremely good break we will withdraw all these subscriptions of our adherents."
Mr. Graydon: That is pretty nearly blackmail.
Mr. Reid: It was serious enough. In Vancouver, the Sun, the Province and the Neics-Herald were informed that if they were not kindly-not kindly from my point of view but entirely from their point of view-these subscriptions -would ibe withdrawn from those papers.
To-day I received from Vancouver a copy of an article which appeared in the Province of May 13, which states:
In the House of Commons last night Tom Reid, member for New Westminster, named the Vancouver Daily Province as a newspaper that had been subject to intimidation by the C.C.F.
The experience of this newspaper provides no ground whatever for Mr. Reid's statements, reported in another column. It can Ibe said definitely and .positively that there is no ground whatever for his allegations. Neither directly nor indirectly has the C.C.F. approached the Vancouver Daily Province with threat or suggestion that it would be penalized if it failed to give "kindly-" treatment to C.C.F. party interests.
Mr. Reid says he knows of his own knowledge that the statements he made in the house are correct. In all fairness to the interests he has maligned, he should produce the proofs.
That is signed by the Vancouver Daily Province. I should like to say that the only suggestion that there should be any interference with the press was made by the hon. member's former leadeT, Mr. Pattullo. In reply to that suggestion, Mr. Winch, the leader of the opposition, said that he opposed such a bill, which was seconded by Mr. Uphill. He said:
I oppose licence, but I uphold the freedom of the press.
The C.C.F. whip in the legislature is reported to have said that he was prepared to "take it on the chin" as well as "dish it out." You find that even the most scurrilous editorials simply react to the interest of those who are maligned. I though that in view of what was said on Friday I should place this on the record.

Mr. Chairman, I must have a chance to reply, and I ask the indulgence of the committee. I am not going to let the leader of the C.C.F. or the leader of any other party make any comment about me without an opportunity of replying.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think under the circumstances the hon. member for New Westminster should be able to answer. Perhaps I was remiss in my duty in allowing the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar to make the statement he did, but I feel that the hon. member should be permitted to make an answer.

The article just read by the leader of the C.C.F. shows what is going on in this country with regard to the recording of the proceedings of this house. I remember distinctly what was said, and I think every hon. member who was present on that occasion will also remember. My memory is fairly accurate on the matter. I remember the interjection made by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar when I made the accusation against the C.C.F. in connection with newspapers of the Fraser valley. When I mentioned the Province, the Sun and the News-Herald, the hon. member interjected and asked me if I had any proof. I cannot turn up the record just at the moment. I said that I had no direct proof about those three papers, but that I did have some proof about the Fraser valley. That is the record and the hon. member knows it. He endeavoured by reading the record to leave the inference that I had deliberately lied in the House of Commons. He just cannot get away with that. He has got away with a lot, but he is not going to get away with anything of that kind as long as I have breath in my body. I will have more to say later about the tactics of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar.
Oh, oh.

You just sit down; you will have a chance later. You are not speaking to a stranger now; you are speaking to someone who knows he has a right to speak. The record stands exactly as I stated it. I can well understand a large newspaper saying that no one had come to see them, but we know what took place in 1935 throughout the Fraser Valley. We had' it on fairly good authority that the three large newspapers in Vancouver were written to and told by the leaders of the provincial C.C.F. party that if they did not give them a good break, or were not kindly disposed to the C.C.F., the members belonging to

War Appropriation-Public Works
that party would withdraw their subscriptions. I have nothing to take back. I ask the hon. member to read the record as it stands.
Mr. Chairman-
Order.
May I just say this?
I do not care what you say.
May I just say this?
Order.
I quoted the record.
I demand that the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar read the record to the house right now. Read Hansard.
I will read it again.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am going to give my ruling. The incident is closed. We are not here in committee to discuss matters of policy as between the different parties in the house. Both sides have had their say and the incident is closed.

We are discussing a
resolution, Mr. Chairman, and the statements to which I have referred were a part of the debate-
The CHAIRMAN. Order. I have given my ruling and the hon. member must abide by it unless he wishes to appeal from it.
I do not want to appeal from your ruling, Mr. Chairman, but I submit that your ruling is not in accordance with the rules of the house.

I will make another
appeal to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar to abide by my ruling. He has always been very cooperative and has always abided by the decisions of the chair.

I am sorry that the rules of
the house do not permit us to discuss the matter further.

I want to abide by
your ruling, Mr. Chairman-
Order.

Hon. members cannot
shout me down. I was going to say on a point of order, Mr. Chairman, that we are not discussing a bill or schedule, but a resolution. The resolution involves all matters connected with the war appropriation and with peace, order and good government, and I submit that I am in order in discussing any
matter which comes under the war appropriation measure. But if you rule otherwise I shall abide by your ruling.

I think we have had

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have already given
my ruling. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar used the word "technicality" yesterday. While technically we may have a right to discuss certain matters, there is an understanding that the members of the committee shall confine themselves to the item before the chair.

Item agreed to.
Rentals of premises occupied for war purposes, $1,900,000.

A number of changes have taken place in the operation and rental of buildings in the west, particularly in Regina. Buildings are being taken over, buildings are being rented, remodelled and so on. How much was spent in Saskatchewan last year in rentals, repairs and alterations of buildings for war purposes?

speakeroldname: Hon. ALPHONSE FOURNIER (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
I presume that my hon.
friend is referring also to the first item?
Yes.

With respect to
the first item the amount is to be expended as follows: Salaries and wages, $840,000; cost-of-living bonus, $145,000; alterations to buildings, $850,000. These are estimates for 1944-45, as we do not know at the present date just what repairs and alterations will be required. The other items are:	Light and power,
$175,000; water and water rates, $35,000; fuel, $200,000; supplies for char service, $45,000; sundries, $10,000. That makes up the total of $2,300,000.

What portion of that will
be spent in Saskatchewan?

We are asking for a lump sum to make alterations to buildings as required. I cannot give a definite figure as to what will be required in Saskatchewan or any other province, but as recommendations come in from the district architects the expenditures are made.

We should have a statement from the minister setting out by provinces the rentals to be paid during the current year, and also what is the policy of the government with respect to buying or renting premises.

War Appropriation-Public Works

The buildings coming under this item are all for the use of war departments or for war uses. For the Department of National Defence, for the use of the army, we pay in rentals, at Ottawa, $65,906.90, and outside Ottawa, $141,365.28, a total of $207,272.18; for the navy, at Ottawa, $24,259.06, and outside Ottawa, $42,093.12, a total of $66,352.28; for the air force, at Ottawa, $8,424, and outside Ottawa, $98,342.50, a total nf $106,766.50; wartime prices and trade board, at Ottawa, $67,580.83, and outside Ottawa, $541,339.44, a total of $608,920.27; for the Department of Munitions and Supply, outside Ottawa, $150,339.78; for government departments, boards and commissions, at Ottawa, $155,855.43, and outside Ottawa, $459,918.49, or a total of $615,773.92; contingencies, at Ottawa, $17,973.78, and outside Ottawa, $126,601.29, a total of $144,575.07. That makes up a total of $1,900,000.
What rentals were paid in Regina, to whom paid and for what buildings?
We have three different buildings for the army in Regina, at a total rental of $25,520.
To whom is it paid?

I have not the names here but I could probably get them for my hon. friend some time to-day or to-morrow. The information before me shows the rentals for the army, the navy and air force and other departments. For the navy, at Halifax-
What are the buildings rented at Regina?

In Regina we have no rented buildings for the navy or for the air force. For wartime prices and trade board we pay rentals amounting to $8,100; munitions and supply, $3,000; agriculture, $10,000; civil service commission, $480; labour, $7,630.08; pensions and national health, $480; soldier settlement board, $1,740; war labour board, $1,152. Those are the amounts paid in Regina in rentals.

In the Department of Public Works, I am informed, there are about 110 seasonal firemen who are appointed through the minister's office from time to time. They were told by an official of the chief architect's branch that during the Christmas season they would get an addition by way of war supplement to the wages which they were then receiving. I understand that at that time these firemen were receiving $95 a month. After that season had passed and February 4
fMr. Diefenbaker.]
had arrived, an order in council or some regulation was passed which took care of some of the engineers, and some of the full-time firemen. I believe fifty engineers and sixteen full-time firemen were included and given war supplements. I wanted to bring this matter to the attention of the minister because there are some bitter complaints about it. There are, I believe, fifteen engineers who are not included in the order in council which was passed. These fifteen have a total of 250 years' service in the public works department, or at any rate in the civil service. I am told that these firemen and engineers work under a 26-shift month and their pay is $3.65 per shift. They have not received salary increases since 1921. I am not sure whether this applies to all of them, but it does to many of them. The question is this. Why was it that when the war supplements were paid all were not included? It is only fair that this question should be asked, and the minister should give us the reason for what seems to be an injustice to those firemen and engineers who were not included in the order in council , which granted the war supplement, after they had been told that they would be given what I believe was referred to as a Christmas gift in the form of an increase in their salary or wages.

I understand that in February there was a revision of salaries paid to seasonal firemen. If I remember rightly, before the question was settled they were receiving from $95 to $105 a month. After the first year they received $100 and after the second year $105. My understanding was that if anyone was left out of the supplement it would be the newcomers who had just entered the sendee. However, I will inquire into the matter and, if there is any injustice, see that it is remedied as soon as possible.

I do not wish to do more than call the matter to the attention of the minister so that an investigation may be made. Will the minister indicate, as soon as he is able to answer the question, exactly what the position is?-because this is a matter that should be attended to. We cannot afford to have men engaged in such work unjustly treated.
I will have that done.

I thought we had pretty well completed the programme of erecting temporary buildings in this city or repairing and extending buildings, but I notice a very large extension of a temporary building is being made at the corner of Carling avenue-

That is item No. 4.

War Appropriation-Public Works
In that case I will raise the matter on the fourth item, or someone else will.

I do not care whether the minister replies now to the remarks I am about to make, but I should like to have an answer from him at some time. I should like to know why the heating equipment in the east block was changed, the oil burners having been taken out and new stokers put in for the purpose of preventing the black smoke nuisance, when as a matter of fact, as I am informed, the nuisance is greater now than it ever was. When does the minister intend to go back to the original system of heating?
May I conclude all I have to say on public works by making this statement. I did not want to raise a complaint on the orders of the day because I thought that perhaps the matter was not important enough, but many members on this side of the house, and I have no doubt I speak for others as well, have found that their health is endangered by the draught in this chamber. I know that this remark is open to the facetious comment that it is hot air that is responsible. Coming from the other side such a comment might be so misunderstood. Seriously however, there is a great draught from the galleries or through the gallery doors. It flows down on some members and I have heard many complaints from various sections of the house. We cannot sit in this chamber day in and day out unless we are reasonably comfortable. Personally I do not suffer much from these draughts, but some members feel them keenly and have caught colds in consequence. Will the minister look into the matter?

Last year we did have the ventilation system examined and we thought we had brought about some amelioration. I shall ask the officials of the department to look into it. With regard to the east block, that was an order from the oil controller. We were asked to make a change over from oil because of the shortage of fuel oil.

Before this item is passed I wish to say a few words. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition acts as though he were the representative of the city of Ottawa. It is true the hon. member for Carle-ton (Mr. Boucher) is sitting next to him at the moment. He may act as though he were the representative of the city of Ottawa, but may I tell him that he will never occupy that position, nor will he have a representative from his party in that position.
I do not think there is anything wrong in trying to do something for the city of Ottawa.
Does the hon. member object to his interest in the city of Ottawa?

No. My hon. friend speaks of an increase paid to seasonal firemen. That applies not only to the city of Ottawa; it applies to other places like Montreal and Toronto, but, of course, not to the village he represents. All those municipalities have firemen and they are all entitled to the same increase. May I say to my hon. friend that the Ottawa people and their representatives are as much awake as he is, but we do not want to disturb the peace of this committee.
"Methinks the lady doth protest too much".
It all depends. The hon. member says "lady", I do not know whether that is so or not-[DOT]
We will take your word for it.

This question has been up many times. The salaries paid to these men are not sufficient. This is not the only case. The government pays less for ordinary labour than does the city of Ottawa. I have not objected to all these questions because I did not want to take up too much of the time of the committee. I think the time of the committee is too precious to be used for this kind of thing-picayune politics; that is what it is. I am sorry that my hon. friend ever thought that he represented the city of Ottawa. We are capable of doing that.
There is some doubt about that.

That is about all the hon. member can say. May I say further that the Department of Public Works has at all times done [DOT] the best it could for the general service rendered by these people. We have all classes of labourers working for the Department of Public Works-snow cleaners, window washers, and so on; and they are not being paid a sufficiently high wage. We have tried to do what we could for them, but we have not succeeded at all times. This question is raised to-day because an increase of $5 or $10 a month was granted a year ago to these men. I should like to know who are the men that were raised to $10 a month. I am sure the hon. member for Carleton knows all about it. I ask him to give the answer at once.
Ask your minister.

The hon. member is making snowballs for his leader; he should throw them himself.

War Appropriation-Public Works

I should like to make a suggestion to the acting leader of the government. Would it be possible for the Minister of Public Works to sit in a more central part of the chamber? It is very difficult for many members who are interested in the estimates to hear what is going on.
Has the wartime prices and trade board any offices in the Birks building in Ottawa?
They still have two floors in the Birks building.
Have any other departments offices there?
I do not believe there is any other department there.
Where did the wartime prices and trade board go when they were put out of that building?
We had just completed a building on Sussex street to which we transferred seven or eight hundred people.
That is where they went?
They went down on Sussex street.

I suggest to the minister that it does not look very well, when you go through the glass doors of the Birks building, to find on one panel the sign "Wartime Prices and Trade Board", and on the other panel "Liberal Association". It leaves a rather funny taste in your mouth when you go through those doors and see that.
I may tell the hon. member that I have not been down there. I do not know what is on the door.

The minister in his breakdown gave some of the rents paid in the city of Regina, and they were as follows: Department of Agriculture, $10,000; Department of Labour, $7,000. Could he give us the names of the owners of the property concerned and where it is situated?

I undertake to give my hon. friend the names of the buildings and the lessors of those buildings leased to the government. I shall have a list made up of all the buildings in Regina and I shall give it to my hon. friend.
When the estimates are carried?
I may get that to-morrow. I shall send it to my hon. friend.
These estimates may be through in an hour and a half.
Sooner than that.
I hope so, if we can get that information. We are trying to get it, and if we do, it will facilitate the minister's estimates.
I will undertake to have a list prepared and shall send it as soon as possible, maybe to-night, to my hon. friend.
Does this item include the rental of the Toronto exhibition buildings for military purposes?
No. This item covers only office accommodation in Ottawa and outside of Ottawa. It does not comprise works.

Item agreed to.
Furniture, etc., for war employees, $500,000.
Would the minister give us the details of this item?

Two years ago this item was $900,000. Requests come in from all parts of the country, from offices used for war purposes, for desks or filing cabinets or office equipment. Last year the item was $700,000 and almost the whole amount was expended. We believe that $500,000 will be sufficient this year. I cannot give the exact number of desks which will be needed by the departments. We are just the procurement agency for all these war departments.

It seems to me that
$500,000 is a large amount at this late stage of the war when the expansion has been cut down very materially. Could the minister break it up into departments or into cities and give us some detail rather than have it put through as a bulk sum?

I am a little embarrassed because if we do not receive requisitions for this equipment from departments the amount will not be expended. It is voted as an estimate to meet future requirements. If no requisitions come in we will not spend the money. I do not know what the needs of the army, the navy, the air force, or the wartime prices and trade board or that of all the other departments for which we act, will be.

If there were not a fair idea of the requisitions that would come, surely the sum of $500,000 would not have been provided. It occurred to me that the
MAY 16, 1944 [DOT]
War Appropriation-Public Works
appropriations of the various departments as submitted to the minister could be given to the committee now.

We base this estimate on requirements that have come into the department during the last month of the last fiscal year. Those requests multiplied by twelve amount to about $500,000. That may be a little over or a little under the amount actually required, but I would not like to get a smaller amount and then have to return to treasury board and ask for further money; I would rather have this amount approved.

The minister has no
further break-down which he can give to the committee?

No, not on an
estimate of this kind.

I should think the minister could give us a break-down of the amount actually spent on furniture under the war appropriation measures since September, 1939. I should like the amount spent in offices outside Ottawa and the amount spent in offices in Ottawa. I should like also the amount the department pays in rentals for furniture and office equipment. I believe a considerable amount of money is spent from year to year by the government in rentals alone. I would ask the minister to give me those figures.

My officials
inform me that we do not rent furniture for government offices; we purchase it. I can give the hon. gentleman the amount spent on furniture since the beginning of the war.
Is this just in the city of Ottawa?

No, for the whole country, Ottawa and outside. The figures for the fiscal years are as follows:
