I have not the exact figures for 1943-44, but to January 31 of this year the amount expended was $433,578. Probably that is the basis of this year's estimate of $500,000.
Would part of that $500,000 be used to furnish the new temporary buildings?
Yes; every temporary building put up for war purposes.

I do not quite understand the minister saying he arrived at the amount of $500,000 with no data at all, unless it was
done by virtue of past experience. It does seem to me that each department would submit an estimate which the minister could give us.

I am told that the estimate is based upon monthly expenditures for furniture during the previous year. That is about the best directive we can follow. We are not buying this furniture for public works; we receive requisitions from various departments. We try to keep down expenses as much as we can, but we have to fill the requisitions when they are approved by treasury board, and this $500,000 seems to be the amount that will be required this year.

Shortly after the minister came into the department he achieved a good deal of notoriety in connection with rugs and chairs that were purchased. Could he bring the committee up to date on the situation in regard to rugs?

There has been a lull in questions asked in the house in regard to rugs. During the first six months I was in the department, when questions were asked in the house, I think we had purchased six rugs for the whole country. Since then I believe we have purchased a few more, but I have not the exact number. I recall signing two or three requisitions, and I am informed that two were for the senate.
Does the minister purchase all the rugs and supplies of that kind for the various war departments?

Oh, no. This item goes to provide for furniture purchased by the Department of Public Works for offices only, at Ottawa and outside Ottawa, for all war departments, boards and commissions, but does not cover requirements of active field units such as air stations, ordnance depots, naval stations and military hospitals, which are purchased through the Department of Munitions and Supply and charged to each separate war department.
Is it not a fact that many departments purchase their own rugs, chairs and furniture without asking the Department of Public Works to procure them, for war purposes only
I would not know. If they do, it is not to my knowledge and I would not discuss it, because I do not know the facts.

Why is it that purchases of rugs and that sort of thing are made by the Department of Munitions and Supply instead of through the Department of Public Works?

War Appropriation-Public Works
I do not even know if they do purchase them.

A return brought down last year showed the purchases of rugs for the navy, army, and air force. It would not be necessary to refer to this but for the fact that the minister said with considerable pride that since he had been minister only a few rugs had been purchased.	*
You do not doubt that statement, I hope?

Oh ,no; but the departments that purchase the rugs for the use of the navy, army, and air force are entirely apart from the Department of Public Works. As a matter of fact purchases made for the year ending March 31, 1943, the latest figures available, were as follows: For the air force, 811,300; for the navy, $14,800, and for the army, $19,500. These are in addition to any purchases that may come through the Department of Public Works. Has the minister any figures before him to show the expenditures on furniture for war departments in Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba during the past year?

I have not a break-down of those figures. To deal with the first point mentioned by my hon. friend, that rugs are purchased by departments other than the Department of Public Works, I am quite willing to accept statements made in the return, but personally, as minister of the department, I do not know. All I can say is that they may purchase rugs in their units, air stations, ordnance depots, naval stations and military hospitals, which do not come under public works in connection with these purchases. As to the break-down by provinces, I am afraid I do not have it.

A short time ago the hon. member for Qu'Appelle asked a question, and the answer was, "Well, we have not the records available." We are asked to pass very large sums of money, and surely we are entitled to these break-downs when we ask for them.

I believe the hon. gentleman is right in asking the question, and probably I should have the break-down. I will instruct my officials to prepare it, but I cannot give it at the moment. Some time later I can place on record a break-down of this item by provinces.

I see at page U-16 of the auditor general's report an item of $400,000 for rugs and desks. The minister said a few moments ago that he had not purchased

any since he took office. This item in last year's accounts shows that a considerable quantity was purchased.

What financial
year is that?
Last year.

That is 1942-43.
I was sworn in on October 7, 1942, and served for only a few months of that fiscal year. The hon. member may be sure that what I had said about rugs is true. I am not trying to hide any purchases of rugs we have made.

I was just taking what
appears in the auditor general's report, where I find an amount of $399,000.

Would the minister give us further details as to the policy of purchasing? I see that some departments do purchase rugs without going through the Department of Public Works. What is the line of demarcation as between his department and other departments for the purchase of supplies and furniture? How is it decided which department should do the purchasing?

The Department of Public Works purchases furniture for office accommodation throughout the country. But what I have said about the army, the air force and the Department of Pensions and National Health is true. We receive no requisition, and have no authority. Then, as to our method of purchasing, we proceed by calling for tenders for every bit of furniture we buy.

Item agreed to.
Ottawa, addition to temporary building No. 8, Carling avenue, $300,000.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
At this point will the
minister answer the question asked a few moments ago by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar ?

Yes. Under this item we are asking for $300,000 for the extension to No. 8 building on Carling avenue. That building has 200,000 square feet, and we have been requested by different departments for an additional 80,000 square feet. This space is for national registration under the Department of Labour, and for the censorship division of the Department of National War Services. In the last year those two departments have expanded to the extent that they need nearly all this new space. After tender the contract was awarded to H. A. Wickett & Company for $332,557. In the last fiscal year $50,000 was spent; this year we are asking for the balance of $300,000.

War Appropriation-Public Works
This is one of the largest temporary buildings in Ottawa. The location seemed suitable for these two departments, because they have other branches located there. I believe, too, that the records division of the Department of National Defence is in the same building. I think this is the last temporary building we have undertaken, because we have tried to limit their number. I am receiving requests nearly every month from different departments for more space, but I have tried to keep down the number of temporary buildings and the amount of rented space. This is the last one, and the contract was given on September 23, 1943.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
When will this building
be completed?

The work was
delayed because of the difficulty of obtaining lumber. It is expected however that the building will be occupied in the fall.

It is my understanding that the Department of Public Works, in awarding contracts for temporary or other buildings to a general contractor, imposes no condition that the contractor shall name the subcontractors to be used or employed by him. On the other hand I understand that in respect of contracts let by the Department of Munitions and Supply that department requires the general contractor, if he is to' use subcontractors, to name them. I understand that there are complaints by subcontractors in various parts of the country who in good faith have tendered to general contractors for work involved in connection with certain undertakings-be they plumbing, heating, painting, stone work or the like. It appears that it is the practice of some general contractors-I do not believe it is general-to go round and try to get better prices-or, to use the common expression, to chisel on the subcontractors. I should like to ascertain from the minister-and I am not suggesting that this practice has developed recently-how long it has prevailed in the Department of Public Works, and whether or not any consideration has been given to adopting what to my mind is a fairer practice-that of requiring the general contractor to name his subcontractors, and following through and seeing that the general contractor does in fact award his subcontracts to the persons named in his tender.

The policy in the Department of Public Works is to ask for tenders after having the plans and specifications prepared. General contractors make their bids, and the lowest bid is accepted. We do not inquire into subcontracts, or those from whom the general contractor has asked 100-186
tenders with respect to subcontracts. There may be something in my hon. friend's suggestion to the effect that, after being awarded a contract, a general contractor may go round and peddle subcontracts. As I am not an expert in the matter I have no personal knowledge. However I shall ask the officials of the department to study the system outlined by the hon. member, and followed as he says by the Department of Munitions and Supply.
I believe what I have said is accurate.
Perhaps we will change our policy, if the suggested one is found to be better.

May I support the hon. member for Calgary West, and perhaps go somewhat further. He is completely justified in what he has said-so far as he has gone. In my view the procedure of letting subcontracts should be completely eliminated. I think it is the government's responsibility to know that a contractor bidding for a contract has machinery adequate to carry out such contract. The contractor makes a bid at a certain price, and gets the contract on that basis, in many instances because he is the lowest tenderer. Immediately he gets the contract he starts to subcontract, and then the subcontractor has to chisel on his employees. The employees are the ones who suffer at the hands of the subcontractor. The subcontractor must try to make some money out of his subcontract, and the only way he can do that in many cases is to chisel on the men who actually do the work. If you examine into the construction of your airports and other national defence projects since the outbreak of the war you will find that -many labour disputes occurred because subcontractors endeavoured to make some money by chiselling on their employees.
The hon. member is referring to Munitions and Supply now.
The principle is the same in any department.
Not according to what the hon. member said a moment ago.

If a company undertakes a contract for the Department of Public Works to construct a building they figure their labour and material costs. They should then be obliged to go ahead with the work. But after getting a contract on that basis they farm it out to others who did not figure in the main contract. The result is that they have to squeeze somebody, and the only ones they can squeeze are the men who actually work on the job.



War Appropriation-Public Works
I am sure my hon. friend is misinterpreting what I said, or is not familiar with the practice followed by general contractors.
I am familiar with it. I have had many headaches during the last four years because of that very point.

If, as my hon. friend has suggested, a general contractor had to do all the work in connection with the construction of a building it would mean the elimination of seventy-five per cent of the general contractors in this country. Very few of them have the facilities, for example, to do heating and plumbing work, tinsmithing, roofing, electrical wiring, and so on. I know of only one general contractor who has representatives of all the building trades in his employ. When a general contractor is bidding on a contract he goes to the metal worker to get a price on the metal work; he goes to the hardware man for a price on the hardware; he goes to the painter for a price on the painting, and so on down the line. He takes those prices and makes his bid on that basis. But the difficulty arises from the fact that when a general contractor is awarded a contract he is under no obligation to give subcontracts to any of the men who in good faith have submitted bids. After the contract is let he knows what his price is, and some of these men are likely to go, for example, to the electrical man and say, "We have your price of $10,000 for the electrical work; if you can cut that by $1,500 we will give you the contract; failing that we will probably give it to somebody else." The result is that subcontractors are bidding against each other.
I can quite understand a subcontractor being tempted, in an effort to keep his men employed, to do what my hon. friend suggests is done. He might go to his workmen and say, " Here is a six months' job that will provide work for everybody; if you are willing to cut your wage rates for steady employment, I will take you on." I can see quite well that that nefarious practice might be adopted by a subcontractor. The practice, as I appreciate it, now followed by the Department of Munitions and Supply, is to require the general contractor to name the subcontractor. Then perforce the general contractor would have to use those subcontractors and you would avoid the possibility of the general contractor chiselling on his subcontractors. It may be necessary and desirable that some protection be provided. I understand that according to the regulations the subcontractor must comply with the fair wage provisions which are embodied in every federal government contract.
'Mr. Gillis.]

The point raised by the hon. member for Calgary West is well taken. It is just a matter of procedure. I differ with him to this extent: if his suggestion were followed it would make it almost impossible for the small local contractor to get any of this work. I do not wish to go over the procedure, but the fact is that when a large contract is to be let, the bidding is done by contractors in the larger centres. In the east we have to contend with contractors from Montreal and Toronto who bid on every large project. I do not think the solution to this problem will be found by naming the subcontractor. I should like to offer a suggestion which I admit may not be feasible. I suggest that the amount of the subcontracts be indicated. It would then be possible for the main contractor to go to the local subcontractors and say: Work is being done in this section of the country and we have put in a tender of $15,000 for plumbing, $7,000 for electrical work and so on; those figures are included in our main tender; we know you can do this work satisfactorily, because you are a reliable firm, so that if you are prepared to do it we are prepared to enter into a subcontract with you.
I know the minister and his officials are very efficient, and I make that suggestion to them. I support the principle of fair wage provisions. In every contract I have seen, and I have read over a number in the last fifteen or twenty years, there have been fair wage clauses. The main contractor is responsible for the maintaining of the fair wage schedule, in connection not only with the main contract but with all subcontracts. I think serious consideration should be given to adopting a procedure under which protection would be given to the small contractor so that there would not be-I am not going to use the word "chiselling"-any of the shopping around that is so prevalent when the larger contractors are bidding on projects.

In my opinion the procedure described by the hon. member for Calgary West is not subcontracting; it is simply a main contractor getting a contract under false pretences. Let us assume that Public Works is undertaking the construction of a building in Ottawa and a construction company puts in a bid. The bidding is on the total construction of that building, on every phase of it. When a company puts in a tender and receives a contract it is assumed that it has figured on every item of cost, and it is the main contractor who has the obligation of seeing to it that the work is carried out according to specifications. It is not his job, after he receives a contract to go shopping around,

War Appropriation-Public Works
trying to get someone to do it for nothing. But that is the case under present conditions. I do not believe that the main contractor should name any subcontractors or firms who are to assist him in completing the contract, because the whole obligation rests upon the main contractor himself, and the government is responsible for seeing to it that he lives up to his contract. But here is what sometimes happens, and I know this particular case. The main contractor got a contract for erecting a barracks in a certain section in my part of the country. Then he goes to an undertaking firm and gives the undertaker a subcontract for the construction of those buildings. That is neither efficient nor in the best interests of the country. When a contractor accepts a contract with the federal government for any project it is up to him to see that it is done, and he must figure on every item of cost.
The main contractor is still responsible even if he has a subcontractor.

There have been some pretty miserable jobs done, and I would not want to start mentioning them here at this stage, but when the war situation is not so tense and we get some of our problems off our hands, we shall be able to tell the Canadian people about some jobs which have been done on that basis since the outbreak of the war.

What about the
undertaker?

I could name the firm and go into details of the transaction, but I do not want to do so now. I cannot agree with the hon. member for Calgary West that the main contractor should be permitted to farm out his contract to get the work done as cheaply as possible. That should not be permitted.

The procedure followed in the department is not exactly as it has been described. The lowest tenderer gets the contract. He is a general contractor, we will say. The next step is that he brings into the department a list of his subcontractors and the amounts they are charging for every part of the work they are doing. We approve or disapprove the subcontractors. The work proceeds and we see to it that the contract is executed according to the terms of the contract. We know who are the subcontractors. We have a fair wage clause in the contract and that is followed throughout the contract. We require a security deposit which we hold until the building has been finally accepted.
I do not see how they can start playing with wages, because we haye our inspectors going around and the labour department also has a 100-186J
fair wage officer whose duty it is to see that the fair wage clause is observed. I should like to enlighten myself, but I have not seen the light yet after the two speeches to which I have just listened.
Does the minister say that the department goes into the various costs submitted by the subcontractors and checks them up?
Yes.
I can see that difficulty might be avoided by that policy. I suppose the only difficulty, when there are two or three subcontractors, would be with their getting the necessary materials and labour.

Item agreed to.
Post-war construction programme-preparation of plans, specifications, et cetera, $95,000.

Mr. Chairman, I have just one word to say in this connection. Before contemplating any building programme for the post-war period, the government would do well to pay their old debts, especially those incurred in the fall of 1939. I have already pointed out to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) that his predecessor, the hon. member for Richelieu-Ver-cheres (Mr. Cardin), promised to compensate the reverend trappist monks of Oka, for advances made by them and in connection with work done on a public stream.. I am again making representations to the Minister of Public Works with a view to obtaining for the reverend trappist monks a refund of the expenditures they have made for work done on this stream during the fall of 1939. I had quite a correspondence with the hon. member about that matter. Agriculture is essential to our armed forces and our civilian population; I have already said and I repeat now that it is our first defence line. The minister claimed in his correspondence that such work now comes under the jurisdiction of provincial governments, but the pledge given to the reverend trappist monks goes back to the fall of 1939 and it should be fulfilled. It is just a matter of refunding S184, which is a paltry sum for the government but a most important item for the reverend trappist monks.
As far as I can recollect, that protection, work was carried out under an appropriation for the fiscal year-

May I
remind the minister that it was not protection but drainage work carried out on the Rousse stream.

War Appropriation-Public Works

Such work would have been carried out under an appropriation voted for the year 1939-40, to the best of my memory. As the work was not completed during the fiscal year the appropriation lapsed and the nest year the house did not vote any further amount for work of that kind. That work was begun during the fiscal year 1939-10-I do not recollect all the details on file-and in 1944 I answered that the house had not put any funds at my disposal for that kind of work. In spite of my goodwill, I was not in a position to make that payment, as I had no authority to do so and the required funds were unavailable.
As regards that part of my hon. friend's remarks where he mentioned the development of agriculture, he knows quite well that we are all in favour of that, but I do not think that such an argument could solve the problem and induce parliament to vote in time of war money for work of a civilian character. Since 1939, the government's policy has been directed towards avoiding all such expenditures and attempting to direct; all our efforts to the winning of the war. Such was the policy of the former minister and such it still is to-day. I am sorry, but my estimates do not provide any funds for expenditures of this kind.

The minister will allow me to point out that this expenditure was incurred following a direct promise of reimbursement made to the reverend Trappist Fathers. I fail to see why the minister has not included in his estimates this small amount of $184 which is justly claimed by this religious order.

This claim is not the only one of its kind by any means. During the war, I cannot undertake to reimburse expenditures on works carried on in the course of a fiscal year for which no estimates have been provided to that end. I do not know whether the hon. member has followed me. The amount had been voted for, say, the fiscal year 1939-40. If my memory serves me right, the work had not been completed by the end of the year, indeed there are several similar cases. This work was continued during the next fiscal year. The hon. member says that a formal promise was made. There can be a formal promise only when work is carried out during the fiscal year for which estimates were voted; you may then receive payment. But if the work is carried out the following year when no appropriations
have been submitted to the house in connection with such work, I cannot see how you may be reimbursed.
As we are now discussing a postwar programme, would the minister tell me whether the reverend Trappist fathers may be paid after the war?

I may say that I shall submit the case to the government for further consideration, but I cannot commit myself to a formal promise.
(Text)

Will the minister
explain what is meant by this programme in connection with the preparation of plans and specifications? Does it relate to any of the plans that may have been before the reconstruction committee? Will he be good enough to tell us exactly what plans and specifications are covered?

The amount
required in this estimate would be for the cost of additional temporary architectural and clerical assistants necessary to carry out the preparation of plans and specifications for departmental projects for the post-war period. I understand that our architects are making a survey of public buildings in every district and are reporting to us on future works that may be carried out in all these places.
Right across Canada?

Yes. We find that we shall need more architects and we are even looking for architects. They are very difficult to find nowadays because they are all employed in war construction and other undertakings, but we intend to employ more architects and acquire more clerical help to look into the condition of buildings, the necessity for new buildings, and so on, throughout the country. We are preparing standard plans for certain post offices, according to the size of the town or city, so that we may be ready, if it is the wish of parliament, to undertake work in this connection when the war is over.
This covers ordinary public buildings such as post offices and the other buildings that are used now?
Yes.
It does not cover any specific programme?
No.

I had thought this amount would be very much larger. It takes in a big

War Appropriation-Public Works

programme of post-war construction, expenses in connection with the preparation of plans and specifications, et cetera, $95,000.
May I interrupt to say that the amount is $250,000 for what they have in mind, though for this fiscal year they are asking for $95,000.

I am pleased to know that the amount is nearer a quarter of a million. Will this cover assistance to projects that will be undertaken in connection with a post-war planning scheme by the municipalities?
No.

I have in mind particularly a request I received from the town of Dartmouth on the eastern side of Halifax harbour. No doubt the minister is familiar with the situation there. We were promised years ago. by former prime ministers, that there would be a Halifax-Dartmouth bridge and we are still waiting for it. Perhaps the minister will take note of that and include it in his post-war programme for construction at the proper time.
That, however, is not what I have in mind.
I am thinking of ferry facilities. There is a ferry which is operated by the municipality of Dartmouth. It carries on a twenty-four-hour service between Halifax and the town of Dartmouth. As the minister no doubt knows, the eastern air command have a very fine airport and base on the eastern side, and this ferry is the only means of communication. The traffic has increased some 300 per cent, with the result that they have not been able to look after their docking facilities in the same way as they have done in ordinary peace times. Quite recently, with the idea of postwar planning, they placed before the Department of Public Works a request that they be assisted in making plans to take care of a larger and more up-to-date system of dock facilities. My question is this: Does this item cover such post-war plans as I have mentioned, and, if so, will the minister be good enough to indicate whether the department is willing to assist the town of Dartmouth, in connection with the Dartmouth ferry, in procuring the necessary advice and plans to bring into effect their proposed development?

This item would not apply to any municipal project or to any ferry projects. It concerns public buildings, such as post offices, customs buildings, and other public buildings in cities and towns throughout the country. As to the request for assistance to the people of Dartmouth, the department is always ready to help communities, but to what extent I cannot say. I shall have to look into this project and see whether the federal authority has jurisdiction or could employ its people, or spend any money, on the undertaking. However, I will bring the matter to the attention of the officials of the department to see what they can do.

I thank the minister. I may say that the people of Dartmouth are not asking the department to undertake the expense of building these facilities. They are simply asking for assistance, to provide them with the architects, because architects are not available at the present time in that section of the country. The people are hoping that the minister will see his way clear to place at their disposal one or two of the men in the district of Halifax to assist them in making plans.

I should not like to commit the department during war when we ourselves lack architects and engineers. I could not undertake to do what the hon. member requests. His" request can be gone into after the war. At the present time we are looking for architects and engineers for the work we have to do.

The minister will give the
matter consideration?
Certainly.

There are two
items in connection with post-war construction that I presume could be dealt with at the same time. There is the item of $95,000 under the chief architect's branch, which has to do with expenditures in connection with preparation of plans, specifications, et cetera, and there is an item of $146,000 in connection with surveys, preparation of plans and specifications, et cetera, under the chief engineer's branch. This is the first concrete example of the government's plans to take up the slack of unemployment after the war. That will be done, apparently, by a public works construction programme. We have heard a great deal of plans for the post-war period. One hon. member of this committee has given much consideration to the necessity of public works being used in that connection. I refer to the hon. member for Davenport. This item indicates that the government now has a definite plan or blue-print that is to be followed, I should like the minister to explain fully the nature of that plan. I realize that there cannot be complete unanimity in the cabinet in that regard; for last fall I remember reading that one minister, the Minister of Pensions and National Health, in making a

War Appropriation-Public Works
speech to a service club referred to the necessity of public works and a programme being made available now for post-war. On the same day the Minister of Munitions and Supply said that public works was not a solution of post-war unemployment.
This is a considerable expenditure, particularly when one remembers that it is concerned only with the matter of plans. I should like the minister to tell us to what extent he is following out the policy of the government in this item and to what extent it is anticipated that during the first or second year after the war the development of a public works project will ensure employment. In Canada to-day, as in the United States and elsewhere, groups of business and professional men and service clubs are endeavouring to visualize the conditions that will exist when the war ends. They are endeavouring to arrive at plans for postwar employment. For the first time to my knowledge parliament is now asked, and properly so, to pass a vote in order to enable the Department of Public Works to prepare plans for the post-war period. As I see the picture, it is to survey the need for public buildings in all parts of the country. That survey has now been proceeded with. If my information is correct, the minister has in his possession a general indication of the possible expenditure that the government, if it is in power at that time, intends to make after the war, and also the number of people, men discharged from the armed forces, and those who will be out of work as a result of the discontinuance of war industry, who will be assured of employment. No one expects that public works of itself will ensure employment. But it is one method whereby during the interim period in the passage from a wartime to a peace-time economy the slack of unemployment may be taken up temporarily.
I believe that a survey has been made by the Ottawa branch of the unemployment commission to indicate the degree and percentage of unemployment there will be when the various war industries are closed down. I referred to it the other day. For instance, if a class A industry is closed down within thirty days, thirty-five or forty per cent of the employees will require work elsewhere. I presume that this vote is to cover a situation such as that, in order that in that great changing period those who otherwise would be out of work, or would find themselves in receipt of payment under the Unemployment Insurance Act, instead of following that course and that delay, will be assured of employment through the medium of public works.

I commend the minister for taking the first step; but in asking us to vote this amount I think we ought to be assured that the government has a definite plan in mind; that it has a survey reasonably completed to-day, and that the members of this committee and the country will be made cognizant of what is being done.

This is one of the very important items of the minister's department. Like the hon. member for Lake Centre I should like to obtain some information on what plans the government has in mind with respect to the allocation of this work across Canada. I believe that the minister's department should be concentrating as much as possible on matters such as these in an endeavour to obtain some cohesion across the country so that we shall know what we are stepping into when the war is over and what type of public buildings will be erected and where.
I was considerably surprised by the minister's statement that he had difficulty in finding architects, because information that I received as late as last fall indicated1 that architects were available. It may be that engineers are not available, but I believe that if the minister would canvass the situation carefully and advertise extensively he would find that architects are available, provided that they are paid adequately and reasonably for the services which they render.
May I suggest to the minister that when he considers this problem across the country he should remember that many municipalities, towns and cities have plans either ready or in mind, and that he should in some way or another endeavour to work out some kind of proposition so that all these plans and suggestions will be gathered together and correlated. In that connection may I say it has been brought to my attention that some of the smaller municipalities and towns find themselves in a position where they are unable to give complete details to the minister's department or to the administration with respect to proposed public works because they have not the necessary money with which to prepare the blueprints. I have in mind a communication which I received from the town of Sutherland, in my own constituency. They say that although they have certain plans which they should like to pass on to the administration, they cannot afford to spend several thousand dollars in the preparation of blueprints, not knowing whether or not in the final analysis the plans will be accepted.
I suggest to the minister and to the ad' ministration that some kind of plan should be

War Appropriation-Public Works
worked out whereby those municipalities, particularly in what are called the unorganized areas, may be in a position to present complete and adequate plans to the administration. The same difficulty does not arise in the larger cities, because they have the necessary staff and finances to carry out this work, but the smaller places find themselves in a position where they cannot do this 'Work.
May I suggest to the administration that when it comes to the erection of these public works consideration be given to an endeavour to solve the problem which has arisen as a result of the war, namely, the congestion in certain parts of the country. The minister and his advisers should consider the commencement of these works, particularly in areas such as in Saskatchewan, which, because of the necessities of war, have been denuded of their population, which has been brought down to this part of the country and other congested areas. It seems to me that the administration would be very well advised to keep this in mind, so that these works will be among the first to be undertaken in order that we may complete the decentralization which will have to be brought about if we are to have a proper and adequate economy in this dominion.

This item was studied by the department with one object. In the last year before the war the department spent something like $27,000,000 on public works. This year the ordinary estimates are down to something like $13,600,000. This means that we have not maintained our public buildings, wharves, breakwaters and so on, in the state of repair in which they would have been maintained had more money been placed at our disposal. We shall have our architects and engineers go over these works that belong to the federal government and make a report on their condition, in order to see what expenditures will be necessary to put them in a good state of repair. In addition, every day we receive requests for public buildings throughout the country, and we are convinced that many of them are needed. I would not want the committee to think that this item was brought in here by the department as the reconstruction programme of the government. This provides for the reconstruction of our own works immediately after the war; it will form a part, but not a very large part, of that post-war programme. Supposing we should fall back into a period of depression and unemployment; we have tried public works in the past, and they are not a cure or even a palliative for unemployment. They can help, as
they have helped in the past, but I believe- and I am speaking personally-that a reconstruction programme should include much more than just public works, because public works coming under federal jurisdiction are limited to certain kinds of buildings and other projects, which we are quite ready to undertake.
I make this statement so that hon. members will not think it has been decided by the government that this amount represents the reconstruction programme envisaged by the setting up of a reconstruction department to coordinate the efforts of all departments of government. This money will be expended on our own works, in an attempt to put them in a good state of repair and develop them where necessary for the good of the public service.
Is this not part of the government's post-war scheme to take up the slack in employment?
Not in the sense my hon. friend has in mind. This is a departmental post-war plan to take care of property coming under our control.
That being the case, is there any government plan under which the Department of Public Works will consider some segment of the greater problem of postwar employment?

I believe that is a matter of policy which will be dealt with in due course. I do not think under this item I have authority to deal with the policy of the government as a whole in connection with reconstruction projects.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I believe it is the thought of the Prime Minister that one memorial to those who give their lives in this conflict might be the general reconstruction of the city of Ottawa, and I am wondering whether such plans are included in this item.
There is another matter I should like to suggest to the minister along the line of memorials which might be constructed in local communities when the war is over. The suggestion I am going to offer appeals to me very much. It was made to me in a letter I received not long ago from a member of the armed forces serving overseas. His thought was that when the war is over and local communities are thinking in terms of the most suitable kind of memorial to erect to the memory of those who gave their lives in service, it might be desirable to construct something really useful in the community. Several times this afternoon the minister has referred to public buildings and has made it clear that

War Appropriation-Public Works
in using those words he is thinking primarily of buildings for government departments, for office purposes and so on. There are other kinds of public buildings that we might take into consideration, such as adequate community halls, particularly in rural communities, which would be useful not only for office purposes but for a large number of Canadian citizens. That, indeed, is the suggestion which my correspondent has made to me, and because it appeals to me I offer it to the minister now. As he may know, the community halls we have in some parts of the country to-day do not fill the bill. In many cases they are fire-traps and lack such things as accommodation for a district nurse, committee room space for men's and women's organizations, agricultural societies, boys' and girls' clubs and organizations of that kind. There is also the matter of toilet accommodation and washroom facilities necessary in local communities, particularly when one thinks of days when the whole countryside visits the town for some particular occasion. One thinks also of attractive dance halls, and facilities for drama and other seasonal activities which might be provided in such community halls, together with basement facilities for games and other activities.
This is the sort of thing that might well be realized if some lead were given in the matter. The suggestion in the letter to which I have referred is that the federal government thinking in terms of post-war construction, might offer to put up dollar for dollar with local communities to enable them to erect adequate fireproof community halls containing the facilities I have already suggested. No doubt in some communities an idea of this kind will take root and be acted upon. There can be no doubt of the need for it, particularly in rural communities. Although I do not represent a rural constituency I know something about life in the country, particularly in western Canada. Bearing in mind the need for this kind of thing, I believe it would be a worth-while gesture if the government were to give consideration to the idea.
As I said a moment ago, when the minister speaks about public buildings he appears to think only of buildings which provide office space for government departments. We recognize the need for those buildings, not only in Ottawa but throughout the country. I suggest, however, that there is also this other kind of public building which could be of real service to a community.

And use the taxpayers' money for it?
fMr. Knowles.]

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I suggest, too, that the money the people of this country will want to spend on some kind of suitable memorials for those who are serving and giving their lives in this conflict would perhaps be spent more wisely and more usefully if a lead of this kind were given. I am wondering whether anything of this nature is included in the item for postwar construction. If not, would the minister take it into consideration?
No; under the item for post-war reconstruction we do not contemplate erecting any buildings or works which are not for the use of government services. War memorials are not comprised in this item.
I should like to ask a question connected with this matter of post-war reconstruction.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I believe the minister has stated that he can answer no question of policy with respect to the post-war programme. We are dealing with public works actually in existence.

I am going to ask about public works. The minister will remember that in December and January I had some correspondence with him, and interviewed an officer in the Department of Public Works in respect of the breakwater at Port Morien, Nova Scotia. In the minister's last letter dated January 13 he mentioned that an item in connection with the post-war reconstruction programme would be placed in the main estimates to take care of that situation. I have gone through those estimates, and I find no such item.
That would not be a war appropriation.
It is not in the main estimates, either.
But there will be supplementary estimates.
I merely wanted to know if the minister still had the matter in mind, because it is closely connected with the livelihood of the entire village.
I wrote a letter stating that we would have an estimate, and there will be an estimate.
I hope there will be.

In connection with the item of S95,000 for the preparation of plans and specifications has the minister any definite proposals in mind, or is he talking only in generalities?

I take this opportunity, at the opening of the minister's estimates under the war appropriation resolution, to enlarge upon a matter I brought up at a similar stage of the session last year. I rise to say a word about the employees of our railway transportation systems, and I do so because, during this war time, the strain, the stress and the pressure which have been placed upon the two major railway systems have been most extraordinary. I think the committee ought to take these facts into consideration. Take the question of ^passenger traffic alone. If the minister will recall, last year I put on the record the figures of passenger traffic, showing that in 1939, the year the war broke out, the railways of Canada carried 17,000,000 passengers, which figure had risen in 1942, the year prior to my speaking on the matter in this house, to 42,000,000. In 1943 that figure had risen still farther to 52,000,000 persons carried

on the railways in Canada. I' am not sure, but I believe there was at the same time a substantial decrease in the number of employees of both systems. Previously they had carried 17,000,000 persons and that number had been trebled in the last year. That alone would indicate how the railways, and particularly their employees, have measured up to the challenge which the war has presented to the transportation industry of Canada.
Added to the passenger position, I had the figures checked with regard to freight, and while figures are not always interesting, these particular figures should be borne in mind by the committee. In the year the war broke out the railways carried 69,000,000 tons of freight. By 1942 the freight haulage had risen to 107,000,000 tons and last year it had increased still farther to 133,000,000. In other words, the quantity had doubled from 1939.
Those of us who have had the privilege of travelling to any great extent on the passenger trains of Canada will realize how little, if at all-and I emphasize that qualification-the convenience of travellers, and their comfort, have been interfered with during this strenuous war-time period. That is due largely if not entirely to the type of employees, who, as I have said, have measured up so well to the challenge thrown out to them by the war.
May I say a word also with regard to the enlistments from among the employees of the railways. I also put certain figures on the record last year in this connection. There have been substantial increases since. The latest figures show an enlistment percentage which is extremely high. They show that from eighteen to twenty per cent of the employees of both roads have enlisted for active service in Canada's armed forces. The enlistments to date from the Canadian National Railways total 18,434, and from the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, 18,726, so that well over 37,000 of our railway employees are in the services.
And the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario will compare favourably as well.

I am not quite as well versed with respect to the T. and N.O., but my information would bear out what the hon. gentleman has said in that regard. That road will compare favourably indeed with any others in Canada. I say, therefore, that these matters, in the general discussion which will take place on these estimates, must not be lost sight of because they show that the railway employees of Canada have played a magnificent part in this war and have made a splendid contribution. It is a contribution

War Appropriation-Transport
which Canadians would expect from the men and women engaged in our transportation service.
In concluding my remarks, I take a little pride in the fact that the first job I ever had was with one of our railway systems in western Canada, and I think I can say something about railway employees with perhaps a little more emphasis and somewhat more from the heart than others may be able to do. They have played a part in the welfare of the country which perhaps Canadians do not generally recognize. We do not always express our appreciation of and gratitude for the splendid service which these employees have rendered, and therefore I take this opportunity, at this stage of the debate, to make this reference to a section of the community who, in my opinion, are entitled to the thanks of this committee, of the House of Commons and of the country.

I, too, would say something about the contribution! which the railways have made during this time of war. I suppose we from western Canada use these lines more than most other people in, the country, and I may say that I have relied on railways all my life for very much that I have had1 to do. For some years, when I was a boy, I took the train early in the morning to go to school forty miles away and I came back the same way at night. The attitude of some people and. of this house toward the railway systems of Canada is altogether different from what it was a few years ago. We used to hear a great deal of criticism of the Canadian National Railways. We were told that we had too many lines of railways, that the National railway was running the eountrj-, that they were too extensive, and so on. To-day, we can ask ourselves the question, where would we have been during this war had we not had these transcontinental systems? I am sure the Canadian Pacific Railway company would have given a great deal in 1941 and 1942 to have the rails which were pulled up in northern Ontario during the depression years, because they would have assisted in the carriage of the very heavy traffic across the country.
We should not lose sight of the fact that, after all, Canada as a nation could not exist without those bands of steel which unite the country from one end to the other. Before the war the railways were in danger of losing a great deal of profitable revenue by the competition of trucks and other forms of transportation. I have always believed that our transportation system ought to be considered as one public service and integrated as an entity. Instead of trucks competing with
the railways for the profitable freight and express, the better traffic, they ought to be complementary or supplementary to the railway systems. There is plenty of room for trucks and buses to serve areas in this country where there is no railway transportation or where the transportation on the railways is inadequate.
I think the committee will do well at this time to express the gratitude we all feel to the railway systems, and particularly to the men who have done this remarkable job. I have met railway men during this war who have travelled thousands of miles every month and who from time to time thought they were going to get a good night's rest but who have been called to take out another train of supplies that were needed for the war effort. Those of us who have been in other countries since the war broke out and have seen the manner in which the people of those countries have to travel in war time realize that we in this dominion do indeed travel in luxury on our main lines of railway. Even in the great country to the south of us, the United States, I have found that the dining-car service there does not compare with ours. The service in our country far excels any dining-car service that I have seen even on the very best lines in the United States, lines such as the one running between New York and Washington. I think the tribute which was paid by the leader of the opposition a few moments ago to the manner in which the railways have been operated and the manner in which the men have given service to the communities at this time should be endorsed by everyone. We have men of all types, races and colours on our railways, and from the porters on the sleeping-cars to the men on the front of the train operating the engine I think we can say that they have done a truly remarkable job, a most wonderful contribution to the effort of this country during this period of war.

I should like to endorse the remarks made by the two previous speakers as to the splendid job that has been done by our railway systems during the past four years.

The position in regard to the Gimli airport is simply this. The Department of Munitions and Supply received a requisition from the Royal Canadian Air Force for a bombing and gunnery school, which included an airport and a bombing and gunnery range. The dimensions of the bombing and gunnery range, as I remember them, were fifteen miles by eight miles. In order to acquire a range of that kind reasonably, it is necessary to use a body of water. There are two other bombing and gunnery schools in that area, which had used the two available lakes of the size required for a bombing and gunnery range. The only lake with an area large enough and suitable for the purpose was lake Gimli. Therefore it was necessary to establish the airport near lake Gimli. A thorough survey of the area was made, and it was decided that the cultivated land, adjacent to the village of Gimli, which was ultimately purchased, was by far the most suitable land for the purpose. It was estimated that the cost of clearing raw land for this purpose would be 8100 an acre more than the cost of using cultivated land. Options were taken in the area, and the department was astonished at the price. Our surveyors were asked to go back and try again. Once more they returned and said that this area was infinitely more suitable for the purpose than any other in the vicinity of lake Gimli.
I may add that the purchase was in charge of the lands division of the Canadian National Railways, which has handled all land transactions for the Department of Munitions and

Supply since the department was formed. Colonel Clarke, head of that division, was in general charge, while the western representatives of the railway in the land department were in immediate charge. Colonel Clarke was asked to get an independent valuation, and he chose the Swanson firm. Colonel Swanson was at that time, or had been very shortly before, president of the Winnipeg real estate board, and, in the opinion of Colonel Clarke, who made the choice, it was a thoroughly reputable firm. It was solely his choice. Colonel Swanson made a detailed valuation. He and his staff spent some time at the site, and submitted a report on values which was considerably in excess of the options that had been taken by Colonel Clarke. A thorough discussion was had. Officers of my department were consulted, and it has been explained to me that the site chosen is made up of highly productive land. It is in a dairying section, and it was pointed out that there was not a mortgage on any piece of land; that all lands were owned debt-free. The farmers were prosperous and doing well, and some of them were extremely reluctant to sell at any price. The owners took the view they were getting on very well, and they wished the Department of Munitions and Supply would go elsewhere for their airport.
Having all these reports before me, and all the information I could obtain, I decided it was better business for the government to pay the price asked than it would be to expropriate, and to leave the fixing of values to the exchequer court. These were small farmers, small holders, men who were being deprived of their source of livelihood and who had to settle elsewhere. It was thought it would be unfair to these 'small holders to put them to the expense of exchequer court proceedings, and cause delay in payment for the land, payment upon which they must depend to reestablish themselves in other locations.
On the other side it was felt by my officers- an opinion in which I concurred-that after ten per cent was added for forcible taking the chances were that the government would pay more for the land, as a result of an exchequer court finding, than it would pay by accepting the options which had been obtained by Colonel Clark. I may say that it has been our experience that wherever we have submitted the purchase of land to the exchequer court we have paid more for it than the price for which we could have purchased it through direct negotiation. I can give chapter and verse for that, in respect of a considerable number of airport sites which have been acquired by expropriation.

War Appropriation-Transport
The airport was built. I may say that it was the cheapest airport among the bombing and gunnery schools. Results amply bore out the information given to me that this was very suitable land for an airport. As I have said, I have been prepared on other-and appropriate-occasions, to supply all the information bearing on this airport. I could have given my hon. friend chapter and verse for every parcel of land included in the area.
I do say this: I take full responsibility for the purchase of the Gimli airport. I am willing to appear before any tribunal and justify the purchase. I believe I can bring evidence of responsible people who have had years of training in the purchase of real estate, and who actually went on the site and explored the situation upon which their report was made, sufficient to justify the transaction.

Mr. Chairman, before we start on the detailed examination of the estimates submitted to us by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Michaud), I wish to make a very special appeal to him on behalf of a class of citizens about whom we seldom hear in this house, namely, our college students. I wish to call the minister's attention to them, following some steps that were taken in December last so that they might continue to enjoy the privilege of reduced fares which the railways used to grant them when they went home for the Christmas or summer holidays. Having been advised by many of them at the beginning of December last that such a privilege would no longer be granted, I communicated, in the first place, with Mr. G. A. Brass, chairman of the Canadian Pas-.senger Association, from whom I received the following letter:
December 8, 1943
Dear Sir:
Referring to your telegram of date regarding students' Christmas vacation fares.
As you know, it has heretofore been the practice of the railways to authorize reduced fares during public holiday periods, such as Christmas, New Year, Easter, et cetera, and, as a part of the general public holiday arrangement, to also accord to students and teachers a longer period of sale and return limit to coincide with the period of school closing.
However, under the provisions of orders in council P.C. 2557 and P.C. 6372, the railways are prohibited from authorizing any reduced faxes for public holidays. . . . Consequently, the customary holiday fares for the general public, including students, during the Christmas and New Year holidays will not be authorized this year.
I regret that, under these circumstances, we shall be unable to make any exception in the case of the students referred to.
Yours truly,
J. A. Brass, Chairman.
Mr. Chairman, I believe the Minister of Transport should, before the end of the present school term, see to it that these orders in . council are amended to enable these college students to benefit from the reductions which they enjoyed in the past. And in support of this appeal, I feel that I cannot do better than to read excerpts from three letters which I received last December and which give a true picture of the plight of our college students. I quote the following from one dated December 4, 1943, which I received from Mr. Paul Emile Tremblay, of the Seminary of Chicoutimi:
We, of Charlevoix-Saguenay, have learned with considerable dismay of this extraordinary announcement. Indeed most of us belong to large families who are forced to make sacrifices in order to enable one of their members to complete his education.
We cannot afford to pay twenty-five, thirty-five or even fifty dollars (in the case of those who live on the north shore) for two weeks' holidays. If we were earning money, the situation might be different, but we must face facts. This is why, to-day, more than seventy-five young men from Charlevoix-Saguenay request your help.
I have received another, bearing the date of December 4, 1943, and signed by Mr. Saul Otis, of the Seminary of Chicoutimi. It says in part:
Consider my case. I live at Baie-Saint-Paul, [DOT]which is quite a distance. This trip would call for an expenditure of about $20 for fare alone, and as I have a brother with me, a total of $40 would be required. Do you think it is fair to have us spend $40 just for a very short stay in our family?
And, finally, I shall read the following excerpt from a letter of December 5, 1943, signed by Mr. Alphee Lessard:
However, unless I can get a reduction, I shall be compelled to spend the holiday season within the four walls of my seminary.
I believe, Mr. Chairman, that the Minister of Transport should listen to the appeals of these young people and take the measures necessary to have them enjoy, as I said before, the rate reductions to which they have been accustomed. When all is told, we should not forget that most of these students are members of large and poor families and I feel that the Minister of Transport would deserve commendation if he had this order in council amended.

The last time this question of the Gimli airport was raised by the bon. member for Souris, namely the occasion when the war expenditures committee was under discussion, he promised he would prove to the house that this land cost the department $72 an acre. At that time I said that that was not true.
Land and buildings.
The hon. member did not say land and buildings.
Read the record tomorrow and see.
If that is true, I have no more to say.
That may be a good idea.

The hon. member for York-Sunbury knows something about taking land, and I am sure he will appreciate that the report of the department states that the value of the land was $45.00 an acre; the buildings were valued at an average of $20 an acre, and forced vacating was valued at ten per cent, or $6.40, which made a total of $72. The Winnipeg Tribune compared the purchase of this land at Gimli with the purchase of land at Carberry, but the fact is that at Carberry no buildings were involved and the average price paid per acre was $43. I refer the hon. member to the independent valuator's report on the land at Gimli. There was an alfalfa crop valued at $15 an acre, and other grain crops which were valued at so much an acre, the total valuation, all included, being an average of $72 an acre. But it certainly did not cost S72 an acre for the land alone.
If my hon. friend says that he did not say that, I am not going to raise any further point with him. But it has been said repeatedly that the land at Gimli cost $72, while the land at Carberry cost $43, but there is no comparison between the two. There were thirteen properties and nine homesteads involved at Gimli, but in the other case it was all clear field. I think everybody in the house will appreciate the difference.

speechtext: It comes under the Department of Munitions and Supply and we are now discussing the Department of Transport.

May I just say this to the committee. I have sat here for half an hour and have listened to a discussion about the Gimli airport. I did not say anything because I did not want to appear to be stopping debate all the time. This afternoon the leader of the opposition hoped that we could increase the tempo of the business of the house. On the point of order, with all due deference to the minister who is leading the government may I say that this' property was not purchased, as he says, by the Department of Munitions and Supply. I have all the detailed documents in the return and they show that the papers were signed by officials of the Department of Transport. If the minister can show me where I would be more in order to discuss this matter than under this present item, I should like to know.
I would suggest to my hon. friend the public accounts committee which is sitting. He has full opportunity to go before that committee any time he likes.
What department purchased the land?

The minister has said already that the officials of the Department

War Appropriation-Transport
of Transport had nothing to do with that matter. That was done by the Department of Munitions and Supply.
The return shows otherwise.

Still on the point of order, I have followed this matter for some time and the Minister of Transport and Minister of Munitions and Supply took me to task for waiting until this late date. I pointed out last year that this airport had only been opened during the past year. The purchase was made in 1942, and I waited purposely for the setting up of the war expenditures committee in order to discuss this matter. That was one of the last items of business in the dying days of 1943 and everybody was-
"Fed up" is the word.

I was ruled out of order and I had no opportunity of rising at that time. I have been careful to wait until I would be in order, until I would not be ruled out of order. I certainly think I am in order now. I have the documents that were brought down by the Department of Transport and I do not think the minister can deny that this property was purchased through his department. I maintain that I am strictly in order. In answer to the hon. member for Huron-Perth (Mr. Golding), I would say that I have an article signed by an official of the department, Mr. J. H. Murphy, wherein he points out that prices obtaining here were somewhat higher than those paid for other sites in Manitoba. I did not refer to Carberry; I referred to a field in my own constituency which was purchased.
This was some of the best agricultural land in Manitoba. The owner did not want to sell at any price, but pressure was put on by the government and they took over the land at less than half the figure which was paid at Gimli. This was much better agricultural land than could be found in the interlake district of Manitoba. I want to find out from the minister if they do not have some system of fixing values in connection with these purchases. I am willing to take any agricultural expert in Canada and show him the land they purchased in my constituency, and I know he will say it is more valuable than the land at Gimli.

Just to clear up the point that has been raised about responsibility, it is the responsibility of the Department of Munitions and Supply to carry out all defence construction as well as to do the purchasing for the
armed forces. When I left the Department of Transport to take over the Department of Munitions and Supply in April, 1940, I arranged with the then minister and with the Prime Minister that I would have the use of the experts on airport construction of the Department of Transport in carrying out my new responsibilities. As a practical way of making the arrangement, I took over under my responsibility the air service branch of the Department of Transport, together with a small part of the time of the deputy minister of transport, who had formerly had jurisdiction over that branch. I am the minister responsible in this case, and this expenditure was an expenditure of the Department of Munitions and Supply. I should like to make it clear that I take full responsibility for the transaction.

Mr. Chairman,
I wish to join the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Dorion) to support the request he directed a few moments ago to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Michaud) on behalf of our students who have been deprived of the reduced fare privilege -which they used to enjoy as regards railway travel. I shall not repeat the arguments advanced by the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay. Like him, I had, at the request of a number of people from my district, taken the matter up with Mr. Brass, and I received from him a letter quite similar to the one the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay has read a few moments ago.
However, I should like to point out another feature of that matter. If the government has taken that step it is certainly not for the mere satisfaction of depriving the people of a privilege they had long enjoyed, and whose purpose was to help our young people to obtain some education. I think the motive behind the order in council which cancelled the reduced fares granted to students in the past was to relieve traffic congestion on the railways, especially during the Christmas, New Year and Easter holidays.
However, last winter, at least in regard to the Gaspe Seminary where I made enquiries, this measure proved itself unavailing. Indeed, * every pupil who had planned, as in the past, to spend the holiday season with his family, went home as usual. Therefore, the object of the order, which was to relieve traffic at that particular season of the year, by curtailing travelling on the part of students of seminaries, colleges or universities, seems to have failed utterly.
This is the point to which I desire to call the attention of the Minister of Transport. If
War Appropriation-Transport

the minister will take the trouble of making enquiries from various educational institutions, and especially from those which are patronized by pupils who come from distant points and who must, of necessity, travel by train, he will find, as I have said a moment ago, that students travel as usual and that this order has failed to attain its purpose. If he finds that such is the case, he will undoubtedly agree to have, as in the past, a reduced rate granted students.

No one was more aggrieved than I at the treatment meted out to university and college students during the last holiday season. The hon. members who have just made requests on behalf of students,.seem to believe that the minister enjoys the privilege of granting fare reductions on the railways. If they entertain such a delusion, let me tell them that the minister does not enjoy among his prerogatives that of granting reduced fares or any transportation privileges on the railways, whether the Canadian National or any other. The conditions under which railway transportation in Canada is regulated are determined by the Canadian Railway Act. Ever since 1918, pupils, students, teachers, have never enjoyed reduced fares as such on the railways.	These special
privileges have been abolished since the winter of 1918, when the Railway Act was amended. Since 1931, the railway association had granted them the privilege of reduced fares enjoyed by other travellers in connection with excursions or on week-ends. In other words, students, professors and teachers were assimilated to other citizens of the country who could avail themselves of reduced transportation fares on week-ends and on certain holidays: Christmas, Easter and All Saints' Day.
Last winter, the transport controller, pursuant to the powers vested in him, decided to abolish all reduced railway fares and, by the same fact, the students, pupils and teachers were deprived of the rights they had been enjoying as citizens of Canada. Under the Railway Act as it now stands, it is impossible to grant special fares to students and teachers as such. Therefore, we have not been able to acquiesce to the urgent requests of parents, college presidents, university rectors, religious * institution superiors of the province of Quebec and other parts of the country, who asked that reduced fares be granted them this year for the Christmas, New Year's and Easter holidays.
You may be convinced that we have endeavoured, by every possible means, to discover some loop hole in the act which would allow

us to take appropriate steps short of amending the Railway Act. The legal advisers of both the Department of Transport and the Canadian railways have clearly indicated that it was impossible to make an exception in favour of students. As long as the Railway Act remains unamended for the purpose of granting special privileges to students and as long as the order cancelling all permits or reduced transportation fares for week-ends applies to the general public, we shall have to deplore the impossibility of granting the numerous requests received from students, teachers, both male and female, as well as parents.
Was the lake Utopia training field purchased by the minister's department or by which department?
I do not know.

I understand that it is not settled for yet. Did the minister's department or did the Minister of Munitions and Supply, acting in his dual capacity as he often does, purchase the Penn-field airport, or how was that purchased?
By Munitions and Supply.
Through the hon. member for Port Arthur as minister?
Yes.

Then
Tracadie. Who purchased the artillery field? I should like to say this. The minister said that in every case the private treaties arranged by the department-
Tracadie was bought by the Department of National Defence.
So was Utopia.

That is quite all right with me. The prices paid at Tracadie were exceedingly low, but the prices paid at Tracadie were ratified by the exchequer court. Certain persons whose land was taken away from them refused to accept the government's offer, and my understanding is that in every case the exchequer court based its decision on the offer made by the crown. The offers were exceedingly low, and I think I know the reason; the land was inferior. But it is not quite fair for the minister to say that the government in all cases made purchases at prices lower than the exchequer court award. Perhaps that is not just what the minister said. He may have said that he or his officials made purchases in all cases lower than the exchequer court award. The

War Appropriation

Transport
exchequer court awards in the Tracadie artillery cases were exactly on the basis of the government's offers.
While I am speaking, may I say that so far as lands purchased in New Brunswick by officials of the Canadian National Railways are concerned, I think they did a good job and saved the country a lot of money. For the benefit of the Minister of National Defence I suggest that when they come to settle for the blueberry lands in the lake Utopia training area he let the matter go to the exchequer court and allow them to fight it out there, because the differences between the department's ideas on the one hand and the ideas of the proprietor of the blueberry plains, on the other, are so far apart that I do not think a compromise would be possible. But perhaps the minister has nothing to do with lake Utopia.	[DOT]

Item agreed to.
Director of merchant seamen, $1,308,240.
What is this item?

This is to cover cost of equipping, maintaining, and operating manning pools, merchant seamen's training centres, welfare institutions, facilities for merchant seamen and the extension of existing nautical schools in our principal seaports.
Where are those schools?
