speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
There is one matter about which I should like to ask the minister a question, and I trust it will not be out of order if I indicate how it has come to my attention. As hon. members may know, I raised in the house some time ago the case of a man discharged from one of the services at his own request and being left without any means of getting home to his place of residence when that is far removed from the point of discharge. The Minister of National Defence was the first to announce that a change had been made with regard to men discharged from the army at their own request, and as I pressed the matter further, an announcement was eventually made by the
Minister of National Defence for Naval Services to the effect that men discharged from the navy at their own request would have their travelling expenses paid either to the place of enlistment or to their home. As I indicated at the time, I raised the matter because it was drawn to my attention by a prominent gentleman who is working with the Navy League of Canada at Victoria, British Columbia. He and others have been most appreciative of the new provisions laid down by the government with respect to men in the services, and he has drawn to my attention the fact that there are men in the merchant navy who find themselves in the same situation.
Coming as I do from Winnipeg, which is far from either coast, I have not a great deal of contact with this kind of thing, but knowing the gentleman who has written to me about the matter, I feel that it should be looked into. He has suggested that there are men of the merchant navy who find themselves in the same position as men in the Royal Canadian Navy. For reasons back home it becomes necessary for them to leave the merchant service. The withdrawal is at their own request; but it is owing to conditions beyond their control, and when it comes to finding their way home, it may be a good many thousand miles, they are stranded. May I ask the minister whether something can be done for these men, comparable with what has been done for men in the navy.

My hon. friend will
understand that merchant seamen, unlike the men in the other services, are not employees of the crown. They are employed by private companies that operate ships and hire them for pay. When, for some reason or another, they abandon their occupation and desire to go home, since they are not the employees of the government, they must pay their fare. All we have to do with merchant seamen is to recruit them. It is a service we have organized during the war to ensure that there are complements of the crews that are needed for the ships that take cargoes overseas from Canada and the moment the seaman signs articles of agreement with an operator of a ship, he ceases to be under our care and he returns home or voluntarily reenters a manning pool.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I understood that this would be the situation; but, as the minister points out, the government does spend money
War Appropriation-Transport

recruiting men in order to make them available. Some of these items relate to manning pools and other services so as to make sure that these men are available, and it seems unfair to the men to absolve the government of all responsibility when the men find themselves in a situation similar to that of men in the armed services.
Every time the question of merchant seamen has come up I have listened with interest to the discussion, and it has seemed to me that these men deserve every, possible consideration that can be given them in view of the hazardous as well as the valuable nature of their service. They deserve a consideration comparable in all points with that given men in the other services.

I fully subscribe to that. We recognize the valuable services these men are rendering, but our duty is to recruit men to ensure a properly trained crew for any ship that wishes to leave any of our ports. We give them as many benefits as possible while they are in the manning pools waiting for their ships or waiting to be assigned or to be engaged for some voyage overseas on the high seas. But once they sign on a ship they are no longer members of the pool, and until they are through with their contract and come back voluntarily into the pool in order to hire again they are not at all under our control.

I have spoken several times on the merchant marine. I think they are more or less forgotten, although they are serving in just as important a capacity as the army, the navy or the air force. I believe the minister recognizes that. I hold in my hand a press clipping dated April 3, 1943, which contains a statement of the minister. In that statement he recognizes the importance of the merchant marine, because he said that without the service performed by the me'chant marine the rest of our war effort w" lid be totally unavailing. It is a realistic sta iement, but when it comes to doing something for these people the shoe is on the other foot.
While I was listening to the minster a few moments ago, answering the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, I could not help thinking the war effort of the army, navy and air force is a protected one. The only section of the war effort that has received practically none of the benefits that the government are making available to the sections of the service over which they have control is that which is still prosecuted under the system of private enterprise. I refer to the merchant marine. That applies to wages,
rMr. Knowles.]
allowances, rehabilitation benefits and everything that goes to compensate them in a monetary way. But the situation is different with those who are fighting the war in the recognized military services.
One point brought out by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is worthy of consideration. Many of those boys from the prairies and some from Vancouver, after serving on the water for a considerable length of time, are landed in Halifax, or persons from Halifax are landed in Vancouver, and they have to make their way across the country without any assistance in the way of transportation.
To get to their homes?
Yes.

Is there
not a distressed seamens' fund to take care of that? There has always been provision for that.
That is charity.

No; I
would not say that.
Absolutely.

There is
a distinction between charity and that. I do not think it is quit^ charity.

In my opinion it is. Those men suffer from many disabilities. The dependents of those men who serve in the merchant marine are in an awkward position. If a young man goes into the merchant service and is lost at sea, or if he is on a ship of foreign registry, it takes months for his parents to unravel exactly what happened. You have to check with the Norwegian consul, or the Greek consul, or someone else. If the boy is a Canadian citizen and he volunteers in one of the most essential branches of the service and goes on board a ship of foreign registry, he loses his Canadian citizenship; and the responsibility for checking or compensating the parents for the loss of the son is passed along to another government. That is something which should be corrected.

I think my hon. friend
has been misinformed if he labours under the impression that because a seaman takes articles on a foreign ship he loses his citizenship. He does not. A seaman who is sick abroad gets twelve weeks' pay, and if he is injured on a boat of Canadian registry he gets compensation.
In theory.

No; in practice.

War Appropriation-Transport

Perhaps I have had as much experience in this as any other hon. member of the committee, and I am still tracking down cases that I have had on my hands since 1941. While the minister has a paper organization that sets up the mechanics which he describes, unfortunately when you try to put them into practice and administer the regulations you are up against a different proposition. If you can prove that the boy was lost at sea by enemy action, you are referred by a department of government to the government that has the ship under its registry. You deal for a short time with the British board of trade, and after months and months of correspondence perhaps you get somewhere. While the minister is quite right in theory in saying that the boy does not lose his Canadian citizenship, yet in fact he does. He certainly has not the benefits that the Canadian service personnel receive through the medium of their own government and through the Department of Transport and the Department of National Defence for Naval Services. None of these departments of government in Canada is able to do anything for him until you finally check and prove your case through other governments. What I am arguing about at the present time is the delay and all the unnecessary machinery that applies to Canada nationals serving on ships of foreign registry. I want the minister to answer these questions because I have another question to ask.	*
There is the matter of insurance. The service personnel in the merchant marine have very little protection. When a Canadian national goes aboard a ship of foreign registry in Canada, or on one of our own Canadian steamship lines, is he protected by insurance of any kind by the company which owns the ship on which he is serving? That is a question which comes up from time to time.
Yes.
I have never been able to prove that. I have a dozen cases.
He is protected on lake steamers.
That may be so on lake steamers, but I am talking about ocean-going ships.
Under the provincial laws of all the provinces there is compensation on inland waters and on coastal waters.

But not
on the high seas.

Not on the high seas. There is no compensation under any law as yet; but for the benefit of my hon. friend I
may say that at the present time some officials of several departments of government are working together preparing a plan of compensation for Canadian seamen who meet with accidents on the high seas.

I am very glad to hear that, but there is discrimination again. There is a private enterprise set-up to employ - merchant seamen and there is the government setup which is responsible for the other service personnel. The man who is in the sendees is protected; his dependents are protected if anything happens to him, but not so with the merchant marine. In my opinion it is rank discrimination to enlist the services of a man or a boy in that particular occupation, because I think it is the most hazardous of all, sailing on those old boats with very little protection and under war conditions at all times. There is no way of fighting back. If the seaman is lost at sea I think the least that the companies which employ him can do is to insure him for a certain amount in order to protect his dependents. I realize that such seamen are included in the Canadian pension regulations now, but if they are killed by enemy action you have to prove the claim, and it is a rather difficult thing to do. It takes a long roundabout course, as the Minister of Pensions and National Health will admit, because he is tracing a lot of them now.
Another point I should like the minister to comment on is medical facilities. What are the medical facilities at Canadian ports for Canadian merchant seamen who happen to land at Halifax, Montreal or Vancouver, or any of our Canadian ports? What are the facilities to take care of them if they are sick and require medical attention or hospitalization? Have they the right to enter a military or naval establishment in those ports? I have received letters stating that men have left their ships in Halifax, for example, requiring hospitalization, and met with a great deal of difficulty in securing it. Finally they got into hospitals, but during the period of their stay they receive none of the benefits that are given the service personnel in the way of pay, allowances, a little something for comforts and so forth. It seems to me that they have a great deal of difficulty in getting any kind of medical attention if they leave their ships under the circumstances I have just mentioned. These are sore points with the men serving in the merchant navy, and I think they require some attention.

By arrangement with the Department of Pensions and National Health the services of that department in all Canadian ports are available to merchant seamen who
War Appropriation-Transport

are in need of medical attention. In addition, we have just drawn up a new regulation under which sick seamen are entitled to an amount not to exceed twelve weeks' wages, excluding war risk bonus and war service bonus, in addition to the medical care and attention they receive through the Department of Pensions and National Health.

Is this the distinction, that men in the merchant marine are not enlisted men of the crown, while those in the armed services are, and therefore the men in the merchant marine have never been given the same benefits? I think that is the principle upon which the department has been acting. Some time ago men of the merchant navy who suffered by reason of enemy action on the high seas-Canadian nationals, we will say, serving in ships of Canadian registry- were brought within the provisions of the Pension Act, were they not?
Yes.

Now they are entitled to pensions, provided they prove their case, to the same extent as men in the armed services. I point out to the minister, then, that we have admitted the principle; and if these men to whom the hon. member for Cape Breton South is referring are doing war service comparable with that of the men in the armed services who are not actually fighting abroad, then why should we not, at all events during the period of the war, go a greater distance than we have gone? I think the hon. member for Cape Breton South has made out a case for further assistance to the men of the merchant marine.
Take the case of the damage to the Lady Nelson, about which I happen to know quite a lot because the captain was a great personal friend of mine. She was torpedoed in St. Lucia harbour; her whole stern was blown off, and I suppose there was some loss of life, though I do not recall that. She was repaired on the spot at least to the extent that she could be towed to Mobile, Alabama, where she was, in fact, rebuilt and converted into a hospital ship. The season of the year was such that getting her there was a terrific task. She was a tow at four miles an hour over thousands of miles of water, down through the Florida ship canal and up through the gulf of Mexico to Mobile, Alabama, and then the superintendence of the conversion had to take place. As a result, more than one person, including the master, lost his health. After some trouble-[DOT] I do not say there was a battle or anything of the sort-upon the submission of evidence as to his health before this voyage, the pension

commission agreed that his condition, which they had previously held was pre-enlistment- I believe it was a heart condition-had been aggravated by the services he had performed.
I mention this case to show that by virtue of the amendment to the pension legislation we have recognized the very principle for which the hon. member for Cape Breton South is contending. As 1 understand it, he is saying that while in theory and in certain directions we have perhaps admitted the principle, in other directions it does not function without a great deal of trouble. If that be so, it is a pity. The minister and the officials of his department ought to make it easier for a man in the merchant navy to show that he is suffering as a result of his service at sea, because that man is really not in a position to fight for himself. The minister should give the committee some assurance that the extension of the principle of liability for injury or suffering or incapacitation will be sympathetically considered, because undoubtedly these men are doing a great national service. I offer this to the minister as a constructive suggestion.

These are very good suggestions. The committee will realize that when war broke out we had to build up a body of merchant seamen as quickly as possible, but practically every week we are able to grant further benefits to these men or do something that will improve the conditions under which they work or the conditions under which they wait between voyages, and also improve their remuneration. We now pay them up to twelve weeks while they are sick. We expect to have full compensation even for both sickness and accident on the high seas. We give them an additional war service bonus after they have served in the merchant navy for a year. At the end of one year's service we give them twenty-four days' leave with pay, and a one-third of single first-class or coach fare, with the remainder of the fare paid by the Department of Transport, round trip. These are benefits we have been able to work out gradually for the merchant seamen. In addition, we make an allowance to the dependents in case of death, and we are working out rules which will make it as easy and simple as possible for the sick or disabled man or his dependents (to establish a claim to benefits from the Department of Transport, which in turn we transfer to the Department of Pensions and National Health, who administer these matters.

I should like a little more information as to just what is done for dependents of merchant seamen who lose their lives as a result of ships being torpedoed. I

War Appropriation-Transport
was following the last war, and still am, now an honorary officer of the Navy League of Canada. The Navy League of Canada was appointed one of the agencies following the last war to dispense reparations. I have forgotten all the particulars, but I know they applied to merchant seamen, or rather to the families of merchant seamen who had lost their lives through ships having been torpedoed.
I have long believed-I could not believe' anything else-that the family of a merchant seaman who loses his life while engaged in war work, possibly that of convoying the goods of war, or goods required to maintain the people of the old country, are just as much entitled to full compensation as the man who does the fighting-perhaps I should not say just as much as the man who does the fighting, because perhaps he is entitled to more than anybody else-but at all events are entitled to full compensation.
I am not sure just what the position is to-day, but if the wives and families of men who have been lost in convoy work are not receiving the same benefits, then certainly they should be. If that is not the case, then I hope the minister will see that it is.
To-day the dependents of merchant seamen get exactly the same benefits as those of the navy.
And just as quickly, and without trouble?
Yes, it is administered by the same department, namely the Department of Pensions and National Health.

Item agreed to.
Joint U.S.A. and Canada defence-purchase, leasing or otherwise acquiring .properties, $110,000.
Will the minister give us an idea of the properties involved?

Yes. This is just a tentative estimate of what we will need to purchase or to take over property acquired or leased by United States representatives in Canada. The title has to be vested in the crown, or in His Majesty the King in right of Canada. Some real estate is required. There are many leases, both large and small, especially in the west, standing in the name of officials, but held for the United States government, and the title to which is to be transferred to His Majesty the King. This is done partly through the Department of Transport and partly through the Department of Mines and Resources.
I notice the amount is considerably less than last year.
Yes.
And is it "acquired" or "required"?
"Acquired"-and it may be "required", I do not know.
Either by lease or purchase. The property required by the United States government is mainly leased.
Mainly leased.
And I suppose chiefly around Edmonton?
Yes, around Edmonton.

There are two or three matters connected with manning pools to which I would direct the minister's attention. I am not sure whether they should have come under the last item or this one. I have before me a copy of an agreement which the men entering these manning pools are required to sign. I was pleased to hear the minister report on the degree of responsibility his department was accepting for the men employed in the merchant marine. I think it is not only the nature and importance of that work in our war effort that makes the department responsible. The department takes men into the manning pools, invites them to enter into a contract, and once they have entered these manning pools they are to all intents and purposes under government direction, almost as if they had gone into the armed forces. They sign a contract by which they undertake to go to sea in whatever capacity they can go, and on any ship which may be assigned to them by the regional director of the pool. I believe the very nature of that contract involves the government in a good deal of responsibility regarding those men.
I was sorry to hear the minister disclaim any responsibility for their transportation from the point of disembarkation to their homes. In my opinion the government should assume the responsibility for transportation of not only those released from the service on compassionate grounds, but also those discharged from the service, and those who return to their homes between voyages for periodic holidays. It seems to me that these men are entitled to a reduced fare for their return from the point of disembarkation, just as is the man in the armed forces. They have no choice as to the port from which they shall sail, nor have they any choice as to the port at which they shall land when they return. They are completely at the disposition of the director of the regional pool, so far as being sent aboard any ship is concerned.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
May I point out that we are dealing with item 4. Item 3 is passed.
War Appropriation-Transport
Item 4 deals with manning pools, does it not?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
No; it deals with joint
United States and Canada defence.

I am sorry if I
missed the item. However, I was on my feet two or three times before it was declared passed.
In these agreements one of the qualifications is that a man shall be hired at the rating last held. My information is that this procedure is not followed at all the manning pools. Reports from officers say they have been stepped down from senior to junior officers upon entering the pool.
Paragraph 4-C of the contract states that these men are to receive wages, board and lodging while in the pool. The practice is that when a man comes to the pool, and it is found that his services are not likely to be required for some time, he is advised to go home. While he does receive his pay, he receives no maintenance allowance, although he must remain on call at all hours of the day and at all times, until the pool calls him. I am informed that when men go from the pool to a Park ship they receive regular annual increases, whereas men going from the pool to other ships, even though they are operated by the same companies that operate pool ships, receive no increases. If they go from one of those ships to a Park ship they get no credit for the time they have served on the other ship. I am informed also that in 1943 all the officers on Park ships received annual increments except one class, the wireless operators. That seems to be a case of discrimination.
I received another complaint about the manning pool in Toronto.
There is no merchant seamen manning pool at Toronto.

I am informed that there is no one to whom the -men can refer grievances, that they are advised to communicate with the director at Ottawa. It has been suggested that the director or some of his assistants should visit these pools on occasion and receive such complaints as the men- have to register. It is hard for them to obtain any degree of satisfaction by means of correspondence.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: This item has been carried. I am in the hands of the committee if hon. members want to revert to it.

I have just one word to say about correspondence with Mr. Randles, director of merchant sea-
[The Chairman.1
men. I understand that any one who has ever written to -him has always received a most courteous reply.

I should like to give a word of explanation about transportation costs. If a man leaves home to enlist at a pool located some distance away, he is not entitled to any transportation costs because he is not under agreement. If he leaves his work voluntarily he does not receive transportation home, but if for some reason or another he is sent home, he receives two-thirds of the cost of his transportation. This is a recent regulation and possibly the informant of the hon. member was not aware of the change in the regulations.
Under what conditions would he receive two-thirds of the cost of transportation from the port of disembarkation?

On annual leave. These men take employment for two years. I am told that merchant seamen receive pay and lodging as long as they remain in the pool, but if they prefer to live outside the pool they receive pay only.
If they live at home they get nothing?
They get no living allowance, but they are free to remain at the pool if they want to. There is no manning pool at Toronto, but I shall look into the complaint about the men in Toronto.

In connection with
properties acquired or leased on behalf of the United States, do I understand that we are reimbursed for these, or is that part of our contribution under the joint defence scheme? Do we assume the obligation, or are we reimbursed in any way?
We simply take title, and the United States services continue to occupy the property as long as they have need for it.
But we get no revenue in the meantime?
No.
It is a contribution on our part?	.
Yes.

Item agreed to.
Railway and steamship service, $3,030,000.
What ships are degaussed?

Merchant ships that are built in Canadian yards and all others assigned to ocean travel.

War Appropriation-Transport
I can understand where it woidd be done in the case of new ships, but I am surprised to hear that there are still ocean-going ships that have not been degaussed.
This item applies only to the new ships, repairs and renewals.
Mr. Chairman, are you calling the details of the item or simply the item as a whole? I had a question I wanted to ask about one of the details of item 6.
We did not hear item 6 called.
We are now dealing with item 7.
What about item 6?
I did not hear it carried.
I wanted to ask a question on item 6.
Item 6 has been called and passed. Does the hon. member wish to revert to it?
I wanted to ask a question about aids to navigation. During 1943 a great amount of traffic went down the Mackenzie river and also on the Athabaska.
That would come under the main estimates.

This item covers aids to navigation for war purposes. I wanted to know if any aids to navigation had been provided on the Athabaska river, lake Athabaska, the Rocher river, the Slave river, Great Slave lake and the Mackenzie river. I was informed a short time ago by a member of one of the transportation companies that a large amount of traffic had passed over these waters and that there had been some damage. If the minister is not familiar with navigation matters in that part of the country, there is no use in my continuing.
Since 1933 the department has maintained some aids to navigation in the waters mentioned.

They are insignificant. So far as I can see they amount to little. Barges are constantly running on to the butts of trees which are piled into the river every spring by the thousands. I speak of what I know. Pilots going down those rivers-I have been down them-frequently have very great difficulty. Our United States friends had much difficulty last year in taking their supplies down to their works at Fort Norman. It was for that reason they began to build the roadway from Peace
River to Fort Providence. But if the'department does not bother about providing better aids to navigation on the Mackenzie river route, I have nothing more to say.
I understand that in those waters we have over thirty aids to navigation -flash lights, gas lights, buoys and so on.
I had reference to keeping the channel open and removing sand bars and stumps of trees.
I will call the matter to the attention of the Department of Public W orks.
The Saskatchewan department of public works would not have a solitary thing to do with the Mackenzie river, which is outside Saskatchewan. Nor has it anything to do with the Athabaska river.
I mean the federal department of public works.
Since the traffic is for war purposes, I would think the Department of Transport would have something to do with it.
There are thirty-eight aids to navigation in the Northwest Territories.
I shall not proceed further. I can see plainly that not very much is known about the navigation end of the river.
On what basis is compensation paid to masters and crews of Canadian vessels for loss of personal effects? Is it on a pro rata basis, and, if so, what is the limit? How is the valuation made.
The authorized rates of compensation range from $70 to $350 for men and officers and $600 for masters.
How do they apply for compensation? Do they give a list of the clothing and valuables they have lost? Do they get compensation for a watch, instruments and so on?
Yes; instruments, clothing, and so forth.
And $70 is the minimum compensation?

For men and officers $70 is the minimum, and it ranges up to $300; $300 for certificated officers and) $250 for uncertificated officers-that is the maximum. Ratings and waiters, $150; bedroom steward and others, $70.

Is $70 the maximum
compensation that can be paid to a bedroom steward and others?

Yes.
War Appropriation-Transport
If a man loses all his clothing in a shipwreck, surely he cannot replace the kind of clothing he would need on the Atlantic for $70. That sum seems to me very little.
I have had no complaint.
How does it compare with rates paid on ships of United States registry?
I do not know; I have not those figures.
Whether the minister has had any complaints or not, $70 seems to me very little with which to replace the clothing that is required on the north Atlantic.
Is there included under these items for marine service the upkeep of government steamers which take care of lighthouses and buoys?
Yes.

What improvements have been made in recent months in, the working conditions, the hours, wages and living conditions, of the men who live on board such boats as C.G.S. DollarcTt I visited that boat at Saint John last fall, and I found the men complaining of working as much as twenty hours a day, as much as nine hours at a stretch between meals, and some deck-hands figure that they received on some days about eleven cents an hour, considering the number of hours they worked. I want to say this. I have in my lifetime lived aboard fishing vessels that go from Newfoundland to Labrador, and I have lived in mining, railway and lumber camps, but I have never at any time in my life seen human beings required to live under conditions such as I found existing aboard the Dollard at the time I visited her last fall. The boat was simply crawling with vermin and the officers and men told me that it had not been fumigated for years.

Yes; but the men have to feather their own beds. They are responsible for the quarters in which they live practically all the year round. When the conditions were brought to the attention of the department we pointed out to the men who were responsible for and submitted to those conditions that they should change the bedding and clean and fumigate the boat, and I understand that they did.
Is it not the policy of the government to have these boats fumigated annually?

Yes, indeed, and we give instructions to the men who live on the boats to clean up their own quarters. That is their

responsibility. We do not send in outside help to clean the boats, only to make repairs which the crew cannot make themselves. The crew look after their own quarters and take care of themselves. If they want to have ideal living quarters it is up to themselves to make them so. I know the conditions of which the hon. member speaks. In some instances we have compelled I lie men to clean the quarters so as to improve conditions.
Who is responsible for the conditions? When the minister says that instructions are given to fumigate the boat, who receives the instructions?
We send the instructions to the captain, but a dozen or twenty men cannot live on a boat and allow vermin to accumulate. If they do, it is their own fault.
Does the captain of the ship hire the crew? Is he responsible for the personnel or for any changes made?

The crews are hired
through the local marine agent at the port.
Is there a large turnover on the boats?
Of vermin?

I do not mean turnover in the sense that some hon. members have in mind. I mean the labour turnover. Are the sanitary conditions good on these ships and can the men bath and wash? What kind of boats are they?
Some are quite modern and clean and others are not, until we compel the men to clean them.

The only way in which the men could wash on that boat was by taking a pail of water to where they slept or in a small cubby-hole between the place where they slept and where they ate. There was no convenience. In fact, the conveniences on the boat, I would say, were out of date when Noah built the ark.

Item agreed to.
Additional harbour facilities at Halifax, N.S., $275,000.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Will the minister explain the harbour facilities at Halifax?

On April 30, 1941, an order in council was passed appropriating $4,000,000 for lighterage facilities at Halifax. Since then, every year the work has been done. This year the requirements amount to $275,000. We have expended $3,238,769.40.

Item agreed to.

War Appropriation-Transport
Assistance to Canadian National Railway Company for development of Steep Rock mines (revote $260,000), $2,360,000.
Will the minister describe this large item.

In September, 1942, the Canadian National Railways made an agreement with Steep Rock Mines Limited whereby they undertook to guarantee the movement of ore from a point near Atikokan, Ontario, 150 miles west of Port Arthur, to the docks at the latter place. The government agreed to advance to the Canadian National Railways the capital required for building the spur line from the mine to the line to Port Arthur and also for building a loading dock there.
Does the minister not mean, for building the spur line from the mine to Atikokan?
Yes; to the main line of railway.
And building the shipping facilities at Port Arthur for loading iron into the ships?

I did not mean to say that the Canadian National was to build 150 miles of railway to accommodate the mine. It is a spur of three miles to join the mine with the main line of railway, and then there are the dock facilities at Port Arthur.
Under what terms would repayment be made?

The railway gets a subsidy of twenty cents a ton for the first five million tons of ore to enable it to give a reduced freight rate, and there is six cents a ton set aside, on every ton handled over the dock, to cover the cost of construction of the spur and the ore dock.

My information is that the company was guaranteed that the dock would be ready by August 1 and that in the event of its not being ready the government would undertake to pay the difference in freight charges for shipment by rail instead of by water. Is that information correct?
I have no knowledge of that.

Is there in the
original contract any date by which the dock was to be ready for use?

No. That is probably the agreement between the railway and the company, but it is not in the agreement between the railway and the dominion. All we have guaranteed is to advance the money to the railway.

My information is that that was the contract between the railway and the company. I am informed that the first contract for piling was let by the railway to be completed by June 1. I understand that has not yet been completed and is not likely to be completed by that date. Another contract for the superstructure on the piling was advertised in some newspapers some time ago, and I am told that the contract for the superstructure calls for completion on October 1, months after the dock is supposed to be completed. My information is that the superstructure cannot possibly be completed by October 1, and if there is a delay of many months and the ore is to be shipped for many months by rail, the difference between rail shipment and water shipment may very well run into the total cost of building that dock. What firm has the first contract for the building of that dock?

These contracts were let
by the railway.

And are sent to
the minister's department?

No; except that they
report to the department once a year.

Does the hon. member
know whether the Steep Rock company has commenced to ship iron from Atikokan to Port Arthur?
I am told they will be ready to ship by August 1, but the dock cannot possibly be ready until October or N o vember.
They have an agreement to ship five million tons the first of the year. I think they are bound by that agreement.
I cannot say; I have not the contract. But according to the agreement between the railway and the department they are to get twenty cents a ton on the first five million tons.

It will be paid for then
in the first two years?

I think I have the information here. I see by a letter that is attached to the deputy minister's book that J. W. Pitts of Winnipeg has the contract for the spur line to the iron mine. The date of completion of this contract is June 30, 1944; that is for the spur line.

Has the minister
the name of the company that is driving the piles for the dock?

No; there is nothing in
this letter to indicate that.

Item agreed to.
29SS
War Appropriation-Transport
Loan to the Canadian National Railways for the development of the Vermilion, Alberta oil field, $313,000.

May I ask the minister
whether the Vermilion oil field supplies oil to the operations of the Canadian National locomotives in that part of -the -country? Is that what the field is operated for?

That was the reason why this venture was gone into, but I am told that they have not been producing enough for the requirements of the locomotives of the Canadian National Railways in that -territory.
Are any of the locomotives in that section of the country oilburning?

Yes; my information is
that in the mountain section -the Canadian National Railways have oil-burning locomotives.
Is it -the intention of the government to continue the operation -of the wells at Vermilion?

This is no-t a government operation; it is a Canadian National operation. They have agreed to test or prove fifty wells, and when they have completed their contract I am under the impression that they are to abandon the work, although I am not certain of that.

How many wells are
producing?
I have the list here.

What do- they call the
wells?

The last report made by the Canadian National Railways to the department was dated April 21 within the last three weeks. The report is to the effect that -the chairman of the company, -the Canadian National Railways, felt the result was very disappointing and the vice-president in charge of research and development has been asked to review the whole position to determine whether formal steps sho-uld not be taken to discontinue drilling under the terms of the agreement with the Western Drilling Company Limited. Since then we have had no report. It was agreed that if -ten of the wells should produce an average of less than twenty-five -barrels a day for the first thirty producing days, the leased area could be returned to the Western Drilling company. So far, twenty-nine wells have been drilled. Seventeen are in production, but -the production is very low, an average of eighteen barrels 
per pumping day per well. In the month of January 8,654 barrels were produced, and in February, 6,836 barrels.
How far does that go to meet the requirements of the railway?
I do not know about that. I am told that the Canadian National Railways need about eight hundred thousand barrels a year-this is about ten per cent.
Item agreed to.

There is an item on page 397 of Hansard of February 11, which has to be passed. It appears under the heading "National Harbours Board."
National harbours board-
Halifax harbour-operation and maintenance of fire boats -and other fire -protection, $178,800.
Why the increase?
We had -to have another boat. We were operating only one fire tug last year and this year we have to operate two.
But the item is about three times as large.

No. In that amount is included the cost of building the fire tug as well as the operation of it. We had to remodel an old tug and turn it into a fire tug. The cost of remodelling the old -tug is included.
Did they put new pumps into the old tug?
No; this is another tug. We are operating two tugs.
Did they put new pumping equipment in the one that is being added this year?
Yes; new pumping equipment, and a lot more, I understand.
What is the cost of fixing up the new boat?

The operation of the old fire boat, called the Rouille, is estimated at $66,600 a year. We have other special fire protection, the cost of operating the James Battle. That is the new fire tug. We have charter hire, $17,520, and the gross operation will cost $71,370 this year. Equipment and maintenance amount to $7,430, and, in addition, we have a special fire patrol which cost $32,200.
What do you expect to do with the $700?

That is the balance of the cost of altering and assembling a heavy lifting

War Appropria tion-Fisheries
crane in the harbour of Saint John. The whole cost was $151,000, which was paid out of last year's appropriation-, and outstanding accounts remain, totalling $700. This appropriation is to clean up all those accounts.
Item agreed to.
Assistance in the construction of vessels of the packer-seiner type, $250,000.
Why should this be a war appropriation expenditure?

The construction of these vessels resulted from the fact that about seventy vessels were requisitioned by the army and navy, especially after Japan came into the war. This only affects the packer-seiners of the west coast. We had to replace some of those, because we did not know how long they would be in the service. Eleven have been built and ten are partly completed. We have subsidized them to the extent of $165 per gross ton, .but more recently abolished this subsidy, because we believe that some of the boats requisitioned have been replaced by the army and we do not think we need the subsidy any more. Altogether we have paid $121,500.
If I understand the situation aright, these boats were taken over by the government for army purposes?

Not those
on which we are paying subsidies; these boats were built by different corporations to replace boats that were requisitioned by the army early in the war. We had to do that in order to have the production necessary to carry on the fisheries. This applies only to packer-seiners seventy-two feet or more in length and of from ninety to one hundred and ten gross tons.
How much was spent during the fiscal year 1943-44, and how much is it anticipated will be spent in the current fiscal year?

In 1942-43 we spent $61,511.55; in 1943-44, for seven vessels, we spent $118,225.80. We have abolished the subsidy, so that we are not going to pay any more money except in connection with those now under construction, for which permits had been granted at the time we passed the last order in council.

I thought the minister said that the total amount expended was $121,000. Now he tells us that $61,000 in round figures
was spent in 1942-43 and $118,000 in 1943-44. What is the reason for the disparity in the figures?

The amount of $121,536 is the expenditure up to date. The amount of $118,000 was the expenditure up to a month ago, but since that time another subsidy of something over $3,000 has been paid. These subsidies are paid during the course of construction, and we have paid another $3,000 since this figure of $118,000 was given.
Then the total amount that has been spent is $179,000 in round figures?
About $179,000, plus $3,000 which will appear in the estimates for the present fiscal year.
Then how much will be spent during the current year?

We do not know exactly, because we do not know the tonnage of all the boats that are under construction. These boats are measured after they are completed, and we pay $165 per gross ton, but we think the expenditure will run to about $250,000. We are asking for that appropriation; it may not be all spent.

I am not at all clear on this matter yet. If during the first two years this scheme was in operation $179,000 was spent and now the whole scheme is being ended, I should like some indication as to how much money is still to be spent.

The amount already expended was paid on the boats that were finished. I stated that eleven boats were completed and ten more were in course of construction. Of course, until they are completed we cannot tell exactly what it is going to cost, because we cannot measure the tonnage of the boats. We are asking for an appropriation of $250,000 for the fiscal year 1944-45.
It seems to me that this is a good deal more money than you need.
It depends upon the size of the boats. This represents the best judgment of the experienced officials of the department.
Do we understand that these boats are being built to replace boats which were requisitioned for war purposes?

Over seventy boats were requisitioned by the army and navy on the west coast; and when the army and navy requisition boats, they take the best.
War Appropriation-Fisheries

They took most of the best boats, and we did not know how long they would remain in the possession of the army and navy, so that an order in council was passed granting a subsidy of $165 per gross ton, which would amount to approximately 33J per cent of the cost of construction of new boats. More recently this order in council has been withdrawn, because boats are now coming back from the army and navy. The navy particularly has been building its own boats, which are better fitted for naval service than the fishing boats that were requisitioned at the time, so that we do not think we should grant the subsidy any longer.
Is part of this a revote from last year?
It has that character, in the sense that we did not spend all that was asked for last year.
You are asking for $250,000, plus a revote of $71,000.

No; the
$71,000 is included in the $250,000, which we expect to reach this year.

Item agreed to.
Assistance in the construction of vessels of the dragger type and the conversion of fishing schooners to draggers, $250,000.
What is the explanation?

The wooden dragger is a boat used on the east coast. It is something like the otter trawler, but much smaller, running from seventy-two feet, up, and it drags the bottom of the ocean. We felt that the fisheries on the Atlantic coast needed to be subsidized and that some of the boats were antiquated. We felt we should have the fishermen build another kind of boat that has been very successful in other waters, especially in the United States. The boat has been subsidized at $165 per gross ton, with a depreciation of twenty per cent a year for five years, to be taken in one year if the proprietor wishes. That order in council has not been utilized by the fishermen to the extent we thought it would be.
There was one boat completed, and there are two applications which have been approved, but the boats are not yet built. In the same order in council we also subsidized ;he conversion of schooners into draggers. Only one has been converted. The order in council is about the same as the one for packer-seiners, except that it is for the east coast, where the packer-seiner type would not be the proper boat on account of the different kind of fisheries we have on the Atlantic coast.
Does the $250,000 cover the boats to which the minister referred?
No; this is in anticipation of this year's programme. Only one boat has been built, and two applications have been made. One schooner has been converted. We have paid only $22,088.
Is this subsidy to be cancelled?
No, we have not cancelled it, because we think there is a great need for this kind of boat on the east coast. We are short of vessels and short of men.

Possibly the reason why the order in council was not taken advantage of to a great extent is that it is not generally known. It was not advertised. It is safe to say that a large percentage of fishermen on the east coast would tell you, if this were brought to their attention, that they had not heard of it before. Then there is the other angle that a large percentage of fishermen on the east coast are not financially able to take advantage of it. A certain portion of the necessary capital has to be put up by themselves.
I hope the minister will not withdraw the order in council, because it is an important step in the rehabilitation of the industry. We should see to it that it is fully utilized, and in my opinion it should be more widely advertised.
What is the minimum cost of a boat to which this order in council is applicable?

A dragger may cost between $75,000 and $100,000.
To answer the hon. member for Cape Breton South, I believe the order in council is known in the maritime provinces. Perhaps it is not known as well as it should be, but there has been considerable discussion about it. We do not intend to withdraw it-quite to the contrary. The hon. member was right when he said that it is not applicable to lone fishermen, because it costs too much. It is our intention to do something, either by reducing the tonnage or the length of the boat, or by doing something for the fishermen so that two or three may get together and be in a position to have one of these boats.
How many firms on the east coast operate boats of this type?

Only one has been completed. It is being operated by Sea Nymph Fisheries Limited. Two applications have been made by Lunenburg Sea Products

War Appropriation-Fisheries
Company, Limited. The converted schooner is the property of the Norway Dragging Company of New Brunswick.
In other words, this concession made by order in council can be made available to only a comparatively few firms operating on the coast.

It could be available to any firm, or individuals, or cooperatives that wish to put the amount of money into it. We feel it has not been taken * advantage of to the extent it should have been. A study has been made of the matter, and we are preparing an order in council which will be more appropriate for the use of individual fishermen.
What is the number of that order in council?
Which one? [DOT]
The one in force to-day, to which we have been referring.
It is P.C. 7580, of August 26, 1942, amended by P.C. 2397 of April 22, 1943.

Item agreed to.
Sundry services, $190,000.

What are the sundry
services?

They include S3.000 for the wartime fisheries advisory committee. It is only to pay the travelling expenses of that body which sat only once in 1943. and spent $37.80. This year, on account of the increased difficulty of distributing fish, they might have to sit more than once. There are seven members on the committee. Nothing is paid to them with the exception of their travelling expenses, when they are called to sit and advise the government in respect of wartime fisheries. Then, some of the sundry services could be listed as follows:
To provide for payment of compensation for diminution of value caused by war damage to fishing boats and fishing gear, $50,000.
Construction of experimental long line fishing vessel on Atlantic coast and operating expenses. $60,000.
Expenses in connection with the supply of frozen fish to the British ministry of food, $30,000.
Payment of war bonus to crews of fisheries protection vessels and fisheries patrol vessels operating in war zones within dangerous waters, $15,000.
Salt fish export regulations-administration, $32,000.
In connection with the construction of an experimental fishing vessel, I may say that on the Pacific coast they have a boat which is
called a long liner and used to fish for halibut. This boat carries a line with hooks of a length of 300 fathoms, or 1,800 feet, which is used in the fishing operations. It was thought that this method of fishing would be appropriate for the eastern coast and we had a boat built as an experiment. This boat is now on the ocean fishing and1 it carries a crew of six. It has been successful for the three trips it has made up to this time, and it has been out fishing for four or five days now, but we have not received the results of the last trip. In a nutshell I might say that the amount of fish caught per man per day has been about 5,000 pounds, which is considered to be quite good.
The minister made reference to the vote to provide for the repair of fishing vessels. I suppose that would be to take care of vessels that were injured.
That was to provide for the payment of compensation for diminution of values caused by war damage to fishing boats and fishing gear.

It is quite right that they should be compensated if they are injured as a result of the war, but would the minister elaborate a little on that? I suppose these ships are operating in the gulf of St. Lawrence or on the grand banks. Have any of these ships been torpedoed or damaged by gunfire?

" Canadian
salt water fisherman" means persons of Canadian nationality employed upon a fishing vessel or boat engaged in the fishing industry of Canada in tidal waters. "War damage" means loss, including destruction, and damage caused by, or in repelling, enemy action, or by measures taken to avoid the consequences of damage caused by or in repelling enemy action. There is a schedule of compensation for war damage to personal effects through war perils at sea. In the case of a master of a fishing vessel of sixty registered tons and over, this amounts to $200 for personal effects. For a mate or engineer it is $100, and for all other members of the crew, $70. In the case of other vessels, it is $125 for the master and $70 for other members of the crew. If a boat or gear is damaged, the damage is valued and the amount is paid. "Diminution of value" means the amount by which the value of any fishing boat or fishing gear in the state in which it was immediately after the occurrence of the war damage is less than its value in the state in which it was immediately before the occurrence of the war damage.
The minister may pay compensation to any person in an amount not exceeding $2,000 for each diminution of value caused by war damage

War Appropriation-State

in any fishing boat of which that person is the owner. It is provided that if any person is a joint owner his compensation shall be limited to his proportionate share of the said $2,000. There are also benefits for sickness or injury, and pensions are paid. In the case of a master of a fishing boat of sixty registered tons or over, this would be equal to that paid to a lieutenant. In the case of a master of other fishing boats, it would be equal to that paid to a sub-lieutenant. In the case of other members of the crew, it would be equal to that paid to a naval seaman. The scale of pensions paid to widows or dependent parents amounts to $800 for a lieutenant and $720: for sub-lieutenant and all other ranks and ratings. Additional pensions for children or dependent brothers or sisters are $180 for one child, $324 for two children, and $120 for each subsequent child.
The minister referred to ships being damaged in avoiding enemy action. What would that cover?
In repelling enemy action or because of measures taken to avoid the consequences of damages caused by or in repelling enemy action.
Running into another ship or something like that?
How much of this vote was used last year?
There are two or three applications under consideration but the damage has not yet been arrived at, so that nothing has been paid.
That is of the total of $15,000?
Yes.
Item agreed to.
Department generally, $8,000.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: What is involved by way of war expenditures under this item?

speakeroldname: Hon. N. A. McLARTY (Secretary of State):
speechtext:
This is made up of two items. As the committee is aware, in 1941 a special appropriation was made for the lieutenant governor of Nova Scotia in the sum of $4,000 to cover additional expenses to which he was put by reason of entertainment and other duties he had to perform in war time, supplementary to those performed in peace time. As the committee is also aware, this year a vote of $4,000 was made to the lieutenant governor of Quebec. Before his appointment the lieutenant governor was entitled to a pension of 
$6,300, and some doubt arose as to whether he was still entitled to that pension. He has not been drawing it, and if the decision is that that pension is recoverable, then the $4,000 will be returned.
Under what section of the estimates of the Secretary of State would questions relating to the custodian of enemy property come?
That would be the civil estimates, departmental administration.
It should not be.
It is.

There is the question of the return of properties which were taken over as a result of the ban placed on certain groups in this country. Does the investigation of , this matter come under another item?

I do not wish to be technical, but it could not come under this item, and it does not come under any item in the war appropriation. It would come under the general estimates of the Secretary of State.
If it does not come under "department generally", will the minister explain just how the McPhee commission was paid, under what appropriation?

The McPhee commission was paid out of the custodian's administration fund. Judge McPhee would receive no remuneration, only expenses, and the other members of the commission would be paid out of the custodian's fund.

Item agreed to.
Commission re revocation of naturalization certificates, $3,000.

The other evening the question of the possibility of revoking the naturalization of persons who were interned came up, and I should like to ask the Secretary of State whether there is not power now to revoke the naturalization of interned persons?

I shall have to give a careful answer to that question, because I have never had occasion to go into the question of the inherent right to revoke the naturalization of an interned person. The procedure that is followed in the event of a person interned expressing a desire to lose his Canadian citizenship is that notice is sent to him in the regular way advising him that unless he wishes to appeal against the decision his naturalization will be revoked. But the practice has not been to revoke his naturalization because of the mere fact of his internment.

Newfoundland, Fisheries
In the case of a convicted person, at least consideration is given to the revocation of naturalization and the deportation of the individual, is it not?
It is only to the matter of deportation, not to the revocation of naturalization, although the revocation would presumably follow.
Does the custodian of enemy property come under the jurisdiction of the minister?
Yes.

I have been checking over the estimates, and it looks to me as though the minister will have to get along without a vote for the custodian of enemy property because there is not an item for him in the *war appropriation estimates or in the civil estimates.
The reason is that the custodian requires no vote. The custodian is self-supporting.

Does that mean that we shall have no oportunity to discuss the position? It is important that an opportunity be afforded. If there is no vote for the custodian of enemy property, then I think the departmental estimates generally, as the hon. member for Saskatoon city suggested, would be the proper item for the discussion. I think the minister was wrong in suggesting that it would not be proper to discuss it on his estimates.

There would certainly be no objection to giving to the committee all the information required in connection with the custodian of enemy property, but I suggest that rather than delay the committee now we should take it up under the civil estimates of the department's general vote. The items now before us are two particular items which have nothing whatever to do with the custodian. I do not wish my hon. friend to get the impression that there is any holding back of information, because there is no information that the custodian wishes to be held back.

If I may say so, I think the minister's suggestion is a good one, that the discussion take place on the civil estimates. In the meantime there will be no delay in passing his war appropriation estimates. But I hope the minister will make sure to remind us that the discussion comes under the first item of his civil estimates.
